lead: In the week of the Resurrection the readings show what the risen Lord does with his people: he enlarges them and sends them. Isaiah calls the barren city to sing because her children will be many. In Acts the Church has grown so fast that it must organize its care for the poor, and seven men are chosen to serve. Colossians tells the newly baptized that they were buried with Christ and raised with him, and that the record of their debts was nailed to the Cross. In the Gospel Jesus calls the Twelve by name and sends them out with his own authority. The key words are enlarge, serve and send.

set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC. Many scholars call this part of the book Second Isaiah. Its message is consolation: God has not forgotten Jerusalem, and the exile will end.

Chapter 54 follows at once the fourth Song of the Servant (52:13–53:12), the Servant who bears the sins of many. After his suffering comes this song of joy. Jerusalem is pictured as a woman who has no children, whose husband has left her, and who is ashamed. God speaks to her as husband and redeemer and promises her more children than she can count.
str: v. 1: the barren woman is told to sing.
vv. 2–3: enlarge the tent; your children will fill the land.
vv. 4–6: do not fear; your Maker is your husband.
vv. 7–8: a brief moment of anger, everlasting compassion.
vv. 9–10: an oath like the oath after the flood: my steadfast love shall not depart from you.
kw: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah were all barren before God gave them a child. In Scripture barrenness is the place where human hope ends and God's gift begins. Zion's joy does not come from her own strength.

In Israel's law the gō’ēl was the next of kin who bought back a relative's land or bought them back from slavery (Leviticus 25:25, 47–49; Ruth 4). God names himself the nearest relative of his people, the one who pays to bring them home.
The faithful, loyal love of the covenant. Mountains may move, but this love will not (v. 10). It is the word Israel sings again and again in the Psalms: his steadfast love endures forever.
vv: Sing, O barren one who did not bear; burst into song and shout, you who have not been in labor!
The song comes before the children. Zion is told to rejoice over a future she cannot yet see, which is what faith in the Resurrection asks of us too.
Enlarge the site of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes.
A tent is enlarged when the family grows. The Church read this in Easter week, when the newly baptized had just joined her family at the font.
For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great compassion I will gather you.
The two halves of the verse are not equal. The anger is a moment; the compassion is great. The Hebrew word for compassion is related to the word for a mother's womb.
For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed,
Nothing in creation is as firm as God's promise. The mountains are the most stable thing a person can see, and even they are less sure than his love.
ch: St Paul quotes the first verse of this chapter in Galatians 4:27 and applies it to “the Jerusalem above”, which he calls “our mother” (Galatians 4:26). The Church has always read the barren woman who becomes a mother of many as a figure of herself, the Bride of Christ who bears children in Baptism (CCC 796). God's oath in the days of Noah (v. 9) points the same way: the Catechism notes that the Church has seen in Noah's ark a figure of salvation by Baptism (CCC 1219; compare 1 Peter 3:20–21).

set: The Jerusalem community is growing, and with growth comes a quarrel. All the believers are Jewish. The “Hellenists” are Jewish believers whose language was Greek, many of them born outside the land of Israel and settled in Jerusalem. The “Hebrews” are those who spoke Aramaic and had their roots in the land. Widows without family depended on the community for their daily food, and those of the Greek-speaking group were being overlooked.
Luke does not hide the problem. He shows how the apostles dealt with it: they called the whole community together, proposed a solution and let the community choose.
str: v. 1: the complaint about the daily distribution.
vv. 2–4: the proposal of the Twelve: seven men for this task, while the apostles keep to prayer and the word.
vv. 5–6: the choice of the seven; prayer and the laying on of hands.
v. 7: the word spreads; even many priests believe.
kw: The same Greek word is used for the daily distribution of food (v. 1) and for the “serving” of the word (v. 4); the verb for waiting on tables (v. 2) is from the same root. Both are service. The apostles do not say that the tables are beneath them, only that each task needs its own servants.
Here the word means Greek-speaking Jews. All seven chosen men have Greek names, which suggests that the community gave the task to people from the very group that had complained.
Moses laid his hands on Joshua to hand on his task (Numbers 27:18–23). The gesture with prayer shows that the seven receive their work from God through the apostles, not merely from a vote.
vv: It is not right that we should neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables.
This is not contempt for practical work. The apostles see that if they do everything, the preaching of the word will suffer and the widows will still be overlooked.
select from among yourselves seven men of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom,
Even the care of tables needs men full of the Spirit. In the Church, practical service is a spiritual task.
They had these men stand before the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.
The word of God continued to spread; the number of the disciples increased greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
Luke closes with a summary of growth. The note about the priests is striking: men who served in the Temple came to believe in the risen Jesus.
ch: The text does not use the noun “deacon”, but from early times the Church saw in these seven the beginning of the diaconate. St Irenaeus already speaks of Nicolaus as one of the seven first ordained to the diaconate by the apostles (in substance). The Second Vatican Council teaches that deacons receive the laying on of hands “not unto the priesthood, but unto a ministry of service” (Lumen Gentium 29). Two of the seven, Stephen and Philip, are soon seen preaching (Acts 6–8), so their service was never only at tables.

set: Colossae was a small city in the Lycus valley in Asia Minor, in present-day Turkey. The letter opposes teachers who were urging special observances and fear of spiritual powers (2:8, 16–18). Its answer is that in Christ the believers already have everything: “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (2:9).

The letter comes under Paul's name. Many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name after his death; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. Either way the Church receives it as inspired Scripture.
str: v. 12: buried with him in baptism, raised with him through faith.
v. 13: you were dead; God made you alive and forgave all your trespasses.
v. 14: the record against us is erased and nailed to the Cross.
v. 15: the powers are disarmed and led in triumph.
kw: The same picture Paul uses in Romans 6:4. Going down into the water is like going into the tomb with Christ, and coming up is rising with him.

Literally “something written by hand”: a signed note of debt, an IOU. Our debts before God are pictured as a bond in our own handwriting. God does not only cancel it; he nails it to the Cross, where the charge against Jesus was also nailed.

A Roman general who won a great victory led his captives through the streets in a triumphal procession. Here the Cross, which looked like Christ's defeat, is the procession in which the powers are shown to be beaten.
vv: when you were buried with him in baptism, you were also raised with him through faith in the power of God, who raised him from the dead.
Baptism is not only a washing. It is a burial and a rising, and faith is how we receive what God does in it.
God made you alive together with him, when he forgave us all our trespasses,
The writer moves from “you” to “us”: he too needed forgiveness.
erasing the record that stood against us with its legal demands. He set this aside, nailing it to the cross.
Every debt is cancelled at once. The nails that held Christ's hands are the nails that hold our cancelled bond.
He disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public example of them, triumphing over them in it.
The believers at Colossae feared spiritual powers. The letter says that these powers have nothing left to fight with.
ch: The Catechism explains that Baptism, whose original and full sign is immersion, signifies the Christian's going down into the tomb with Christ to rise to new life, and it cites this verse (CCC 628, in substance). The Church of the East has always venerated the Cross as the sign of Christ's victory. The Cross here is not only the place of suffering; it is where the debt was cancelled and the powers were overcome.

set: This is the beginning of the second of the five great discourses in Matthew's Gospel, the missionary discourse. Just before it, Jesus saw the crowds “like sheep without a shepherd” and told the disciples to pray for labourers for the harvest (9:36–38). Now he sends those very disciples.

Only here does Matthew call them “apostles”. The command to go only to Israel will be widened after the Resurrection, when the risen Lord sends the eleven to all nations (28:19). That is one reason the Church reads this passage in the week of the Resurrection.
str: v. 1: the Twelve receive authority.
vv. 2–4: their names.
vv. 5–6: go to the lost sheep of Israel.
vv. 7–8: preach and heal; give as you received.
vv. 9–10: travel light.
vv. 11–13: the worthy house; the greeting of peace.
vv. 14–15: when a town will not listen.
kw: One who is sent with the authority of the sender. The Syriac word for apostle is šlīḥā, from a root meaning to send, which is why Syro-Malabar Christians speak of the Shliha, Mar Thoma Shliha.
Jesus gives the Twelve a share of his own authority over unclean spirits and every sickness. Their power is his, not their own.
The Hebrew greeting šālôm. It is more than good wishes: it is the blessing of God's order and wholeness, and the disciples carry it into every house they enter.
vv: Then Jesus summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to cure every disease and every sickness.
The same words were used of Jesus' own work just before (9:35). The disciples are to do what he does.
first, Simon, also known as Peter,
Peter is named “first”, not only because he was called first. Matthew gives him a place at the head of the Twelve (CCC 552).
Thomas and Matthew the tax collector;

Our father in faith, Thomas, stands in the list beside a former tax collector. The Twelve were not chosen for their likeness to one another. Simon “the Cananaean” (v. 4) probably means “the zealous one”; Luke calls him Simon the Zealot (Luke 6:15).
You received without payment; give without payment.
The whole mission rests on this sentence. What the disciples have was a gift; they may not sell it.
If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.
Peace is never wasted. If it is refused, it comes back to the one who gave it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus chose the Twelve to be with him and to share in his mission, and gave them a share in his authority (CCC 551). The apostles were sent as he was sent by the Father, and the Church is apostolic because she is still founded on them and still sent by Christ (CCC 857–858). The instruction to take nothing for the road has been read through the ages as a call to trust God's providence and to preach the Gospel without seeking gain.

qa: Why did Jesus tell the Twelve to go only to Israel?

Matthew follows the order of God's plan: the promises were given to Israel first, and Jesus came first to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (15:24). This is not a rejection of the nations. After the Resurrection the risen Lord sends the same apostles to “all nations” (28:19). Paul keeps the same order: “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).
Were the seven men in Acts 6 the first deacons?

Acts does not call them deacons, and their work soon included preaching. But the laying on of hands, the prayer and the task of service led the early Church to see them as the first deacons, and this has remained the common Catholic reading.
rite: In the Syro-Malabar Church the deacon is called shemmashan, from the Syriac word for one who serves. In the Holy Qurbana he serves at the altar, proclaims the Gospel in many places and leads the people's responses. Today's reading from Acts shows where his ministry began: in care for widows and in prayer. The Gospel too is close to us. Thomas is named among the Twelve, and our Church keeps the tradition that he came to the land of Kerala as one sent by the Lord.
study: Isaiah tells Zion to sing before her children are born. What promise of God am I asked to rejoice in before I see it fulfilled?
In Acts the Church solved a quarrel by listening, sharing tasks and praying. What can my parish or family learn from this?
What does it mean for me that the record of my sins was nailed to the Cross?
“You received without payment; give without payment.” What have I received that I am keeping to myself?

lead: On the Friday of the week of the Resurrection the Church of the East keeps the feast of all the martyrs. The day joins the Lord's victory over death to the courage of those who died for him. Azariah blesses God from inside the furnace. Stephen stands before the council with a face like an angel's. Hebrews calls up the ancestors who “received approval” by faith, and the Greek word there comes from the same root as martyr. In the Gospel Jesus tells his disciples three times not to be afraid and promises to acknowledge before his Father those who acknowledge him. The key words are witness, fear not and acknowledge.

set: King Nebuchadnezzar has set up a golden statue and commanded all to worship it. Three young Jews, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, refuse. Even if God does not rescue them, they say, they will not serve the king's gods (3:18). They are bound and thrown into the furnace (3:23).

At this point Catholic Bibles contain a long passage, numbered 3:24–90, that is found in the ancient Greek translations of Daniel but not in the Aramaic text: the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men. The Catholic and Orthodox Churches receive it as inspired Scripture; many Protestant Bibles place it among the Apocrypha. Azariah is the Hebrew name of the one the Babylonians called Abednego (1:7).
The prayer is spoken in the fire, but it is not a cry for personal rescue. It is a confession for the whole people, like the prayers in Daniel 9 and Baruch 1–3: God is just, and Israel has sinned.
str: v. 25: Azariah stands in the fire and prays aloud.
v. 26: the opening blessing of God and his name.
vv. 27–28: all God's works and judgments are true.
vv. 29–30: the confession: we have sinned and not obeyed.
v. 31: all that has come upon us was a true judgment. The prayer goes on to plead for mercy (vv. 32–45), and the angel of the Lord comes down into the furnace (vv. 49–50).
kw: The name means “the Lord has helped”. The Babylonians gave him a new name, but in the furnace he prays under the name his parents gave him, the name that confesses Israel's God.
The prayer opens with the Jewish form of blessing: “Blessed are you, O Lord”. To bless God is to give him thanks and praise for who he is. Azariah does this before there is any sign of help.
Azariah prays to the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. In exile, with no Temple, no king and no sacrifice, the memory of the ancestors and their covenant is what holds the people together.
vv: Then Azariah stood still in the fire and prayed aloud:
Fire is the last place one expects to hear a prayer of praise. Early Christian writers, St Cyprian among them, held up the three young men as models for those facing martyrdom (in substance).
Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our ancestors, and worthy of praise; and glorious is your name forever!
For you are just in all you have done; all your works are true and your ways right,
Azariah does not accuse God. Suffering has not made him doubt God's justice; it has made him look at his people's sins.
For we have sinned and broken your law in turning away from you;
The three young men had not bowed to the statue, yet Azariah says “we”. The righteous do not separate themselves from the people when they pray.
So all that you have brought upon us, and all that you have done to us, you have done by a true judgment.
This humble confession prepares for the plea that follows: that a contrite heart and a humble spirit may be accepted in place of the Temple sacrifices (3:39).
ch: Hebrews 11:34 praises those who “quenched raging fire”, and the Church has always counted the three young men among the witnesses of faith. Some of the earliest Christian paintings in the catacombs of Rome show them standing unharmed in the furnace with arms raised in prayer. Many early Christian writers saw in the fourth figure in the fire (3:92) a sign of the Son of God present with those who suffer for him (in substance). The Song of the Three that follows the prayer, with its call to all creation to bless the Lord, is sung in the morning prayer of many Churches to this day.

set: Stephen was the first named among the seven chosen to serve (6:5). Now Luke shows him doing more than serving tables: he works signs and argues with wisdom. His opponents come from a Greek-speaking synagogue (or synagogues) in Jerusalem made up of Jews from abroad: from Cyrene and Alexandria in Africa, and from Cilicia and Asia in Asia Minor. Saul of Tarsus came from Cilicia, and he will appear at Stephen's death (7:58).

Luke tells Stephen's trial so that it echoes the trial of Jesus: false witnesses, a charge about the Temple, the council of the elders. Stephen is Jewish, as are his accusers, his judges and the first believers. The conflict is among Jews about Jesus, and it is not a story of “the Jews” against Christians.
str: v. 8: Stephen full of grace and power.
vv. 9–10: debate; no one can withstand his wisdom.
vv. 11–12: men are put up to accuse him; he is seized and brought to the council.
vv. 13–14: false witnesses: the Temple and the law.
v. 15: his face like an angel's.
kw: Stephen is “full of grace and power”, just as he was “full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (6:5). Luke shows that the gifts of the risen Lord fill the servant as much as the apostles.
The supreme council in Jerusalem, made up of chief priests, elders and scribes. Jesus stood before the same council (Luke 22:66).
Paul later calls Stephen “your witness” (22:20). The Greek word for witness came to mean one who bears witness with his blood, a martyr. Stephen is honoured as the first martyr, the protomartyr.
vv: Stephen, full of grace and power, did great wonders and signs among the people.
But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.
Jesus had promised this: “I will give you words and a wisdom that none of your opponents will be able to withstand” (Luke 21:15).
They set up false witnesses who said, “This man never stops saying things against this holy place and the law;
The words echo the false witness against Jesus about destroying the Temple (Mark 14:57–58). Luke wants us to see the disciple walking the road of his Master.
And all who sat in the council looked intently at him, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

Stephen is accused of speaking against Moses, and his face shines as Moses' face shone when he came down from the mountain (Exodus 34:29–35). The accused man carries the very glory he is said to despise.
ch: Stephen's death in the next chapter completes the likeness to Christ: he sees the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (7:56), commends his spirit to the Lord Jesus (7:59) and prays for those who stone him (7:60). The Church has always honoured him as the first martyr. In him she sees what a martyr is: one who is not only killed for Christ but who forgives as Christ forgave.

set: The Letter to the Hebrews is a long sermon to Christians who were growing weary under pressure and loss (10:32–39). Its author is not named. The ancient Church debated who wrote it; Origen said that only God knows who wrote it (in substance, as Eusebius reports). The Church receives it as inspired Scripture.

Chapter 11 opens with a description of faith (11:1) and then walks through the great figures of Israel's story, each introduced by the words “by faith”. The list ends with those who suffered, were tortured and killed (11:35–38), and the next chapter calls them “so great a cloud of witnesses” (12:1).
str: v. 3: faith understands creation by the word of God.
v. 4: Abel.
vv. 5–6: Enoch; without faith it is impossible to please God.
v. 7: Noah.
vv. 8–10: Abraham the traveller, looking for the city whose builder is God.
kw: In Hebrews faith is trust that holds on to what is promised and not yet seen. It looks forward, and it acts: Abel offers, Noah builds, Abraham sets out.

Literally “was witnessed to”. The verb comes from the same root as martys, witness. God bears witness to those who trust him (vv. 2, 4, 5). On the feast of martyrs we see the two sides: they bore witness to God, and God bears witness to them.
Abraham lived in tents, which have no foundations. He looked for a city that has them (v. 10). The life of faith is lived in tents while it waits for the lasting city.
vv: By faith we understand that the worlds were prepared by the word of God,
The list begins before Abel, with creation itself. To believe in the Creator is the first act of faith.
he died, but through his faith he still speaks.
Abel is the first righteous man to die at the hands of another. Jesus names him first among the innocent whose blood was shed (Matthew 23:35). His death was not the end of his witness.
And without faith it is impossible to please God, for whoever would approach him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.
and he set out, not knowing where he was going.
Abraham's faith is a road, not a map. He obeys first and learns the way as he walks.
For he looked forward to the city that has foundations, whose architect and builder is God.
ch: The Catechism points to this chapter as the great eulogy of the faith of Israel's ancestors, laying special stress on Abraham (CCC 145). It quotes verse 6 when it teaches that faith is necessary for salvation (CCC 161). The martyrs stand at the end of this long line. Their faith, like Abraham's, set out without seeing the end of the road, and they now belong to the cloud of witnesses who surround the Church as she runs her race (12:1).

set: This passage comes from the missionary discourse of Matthew 10. Jesus has just warned the Twelve that they will be handed over to councils, flogged and hated (10:17–22), and that the disciple will be treated as the teacher was (10:24–25). Now he tells them three times not to fear (vv. 26, 28, 31). Matthew wrote for a Church that already knew persecution.
str: vv. 26–27: what is hidden will be revealed; proclaim it from the housetops.
v. 28: whom to fear and whom not to fear.
vv. 29–31: the sparrows and the hairs of your head.
vv. 32–33: acknowledging and denying.
kw: To declare openly that one belongs to Jesus. The Church calls those who suffered for this public confession confessors, and those who died for it martyrs.
A small copper coin. Luke has five sparrows sold for two pennies (Luke 12:6). The cheapest thing in the market does not fall without the Father.

From the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once a place of terrible idolatry (Jeremiah 7:31). In the Gospels it names final loss. Jesus speaks of it not to frighten his disciples into silence, but so that they will fear nothing else.
vv: So have no fear of them; for nothing is covered up that will not be uncovered,
Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
The one to fear is God, the judge, not the persecutor. The persecutor's power ends at the body; God holds the whole person. Fear of God, rightly understood, sets a person above every other fear.
Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
Jesus does not promise that the sparrow will not fall. He promises that it will not fall without the Father.
And even the hairs of your head are all counted.
Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven;
The martyr's confession on earth is answered by Christ's confession of him in heaven.
ch: The Catechism calls martyrdom “the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith”, a witness even unto death (CCC 2473). It recalls that the Church has carefully gathered the records of those who persevered to the end, and quotes St Ignatius of Antioch on his way to death in Rome: it is better for him to die in Christ Jesus than to reign over the ends of the earth (CCC 2474). Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is a seed (Apology 50, in substance): the more they were cut down, the more they grew.

qa: Why is the feast of the martyrs kept in the week of the Resurrection?

The martyrs share most closely in the death of Christ, and so they share in his victory. In the Church of the East this Friday recalls above all the great persecution in Persia in the fourth century, when the Catholicos Mar Shimun bar Sabba'e and many companions were put to death, according to tradition on a Good Friday. Placing their feast in Easter week says that their death was not a defeat.
Is the Prayer of Azariah really part of the Bible?

Yes, for Catholics. It belongs to the Greek form of Daniel, which the Church received from the beginning, and the Council of Trent listed Daniel among the sacred books in the form read in the Church. It is not found in the Aramaic text, so many Protestant Bibles print it separately or leave it out.
In Matthew 10:28, who is the one we should fear?

Most interpreters, with the main Catholic tradition, understand it to be God, the judge of soul and body. Jesus does not mean a slavish dread. He means the holy fear that puts God first, and he goes straight on to speak of the Father who counts the hairs of our head (vv. 29–31).
rite: In the East Syriac tradition this is the Friday of the Confessors, the feast of all the sahde, the martyrs. The Church of the East, to which our Church was joined for centuries, suffered terribly under the Persian king Shapur II. Mar Shimun bar Sabba'e, Catholicos of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, refused to deny Christ and was put to death with a great company of bishops, priests and faithful. Our own Church remembers that its father in faith, Mar Thoma Shliha, gave his life for Christ in India. Today we pray for Christians who suffer for their faith in many lands, and for those who wrong them, as Stephen prayed for his.
study: Azariah blessed God from inside the fire. What would it mean for me to praise God in the middle of a trial, before it ends?
Stephen's face shone when he was falsely accused. How do I respond when I am misjudged?
Abraham “set out, not knowing where he was going”. Where is God asking me to take a step without seeing the whole road?
Jesus says three times, “Do not be afraid.” What fear keeps me from acknowledging him before others?

lead: The Saturday of the week of the Resurrection brings us back to the empty tomb, and then lifts our eyes upward. Mark tells of the women who came with spices on the first day of the week and found a young man in white where they expected a body. Colossians draws the conclusion for the baptized: if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, for your life is hidden with him. One reading tells what happened at the tomb; the other tells what it means for the way we live. The key words are raised, seek and hidden.

r.h: Seek the things that are above
set: These four verses are the hinge of the Letter to the Colossians. Chapters 1–2 have shown who Christ is and what Baptism has done: the believers were buried with him and raised with him (2:12). From 3:5 the letter turns to daily life: what to put to death, what to put on, how to live at home. The bridge between them is this short passage. Christian conduct grows out of what has already happened to us in Christ.
The teachers at Colossae urged rules about food and festivals and the worship of angels (2:16–23). The answer is not a new set of rules but a new direction: look to where Christ is.
str: v. 1: if raised with Christ, seek what is above, where Christ is seated.
v. 2: set your minds there.
v. 3: you have died; your life is hidden with Christ in God.
v. 4: when Christ appears, you will appear with him in glory.
kw: Not a place among the stars but the realm where Christ reigns with the Father. To seek it is to take one's measure from Christ rather than from what passes away.
The perfect tense: it has been hidden and remains so. Our true life is real now, but it is not yet visible. It is kept safe, as treasure is hidden to protect it.
The word for Christ's coming at the end. What is hidden now will be shown, and we will be shown with him.
vv: So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
“If” here means “since”. The writer does not doubt that they were raised; he builds on it. “Seated at the right hand” comes from Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often echoed in the New.
Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth,
This is not contempt for creation, which the same letter says was made in Christ and for him (1:16). “Things on earth” here means the list that follows in v. 5: what belongs to the old life.
for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
When Christ who is your life is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory.
Christ is not only the giver of our life; he is our life.
ch: The Catechism teaches that, united with Christ by Baptism, believers already truly share in the heavenly life of the risen Christ, but that this life remains hidden with Christ in God until he appears (CCC 1003, quoting this passage). The Church reads these verses at the feast of the Resurrection in many traditions. They are the Easter programme for the Christian life: we live on earth with our hearts where Christ is, and so we work on earth with hope.

r.h: He has been raised; he is not here
set: Mark has told us that some women watched the crucifixion from a distance (15:40–41) and saw where the body was laid (15:47). Now three of them return when the sabbath is over, with spices to anoint the body. They expect a corpse and a heavy stone. They find neither.

In the oldest Greek manuscripts the Gospel of Mark ends at v. 8. The verses that follow in our Bibles (16:9–20) were added early and are received by the Church as inspired and canonical Scripture. Some manuscripts also add a short ending after v. 8, which the NRSV prints in brackets.
str: vv. 1–2: the women come at sunrise on the first day of the week.
v. 3: their worry about the stone.
v. 4: the stone already rolled back.
vv. 5–7: the young man in white and his message.
v. 8: flight, fear and silence.
kw: Mark does not call him an angel, but his white robe and his message show that he comes from God. Mark used the same word for the young man who ran away naked when Jesus was arrested (14:51–52). Many readers have noticed the contrast: one young man fled in shame, and this one sits robed in white.
A passive verb: God has raised him. The New Testament speaks both of Jesus rising and of the Father raising him (CCC 648–649).
In Greek the Gospel's last words are literally “they were afraid, for”. It is a startling ending. The fear is the holy fear of those who have met the work of God.
vv: They had been saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance to the tomb?”
They came anyway. Love set out before it knew how the obstacle would be removed.
Do not be alarmed; you are looking for Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here.
The risen one is the same Jesus of Nazareth who was crucified. The Resurrection does not erase the Cross; the crucified one is the one who lives.
But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going ahead of you to Galilee;
And Peter: the one who denied him three times is named. The message of Easter begins with mercy to the one who fell furthest.
So they went out and fled from the tomb, for terror and amazement had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
The silence cannot be the end, since we are reading the Gospel. The women's message did reach the disciples, and so it reached us.
ch: The Catechism notes that Mary Magdalene and the holy women were the first to encounter the Risen One, so that the women were the first messengers of the Resurrection, even to the apostles (CCC 641). St Thomas Aquinas, commenting on John, called Mary Magdalene the apostle of the apostles (in substance). The day of the women's visit, “the first day of the week”, became the Lord's Day, the day on which the Church gathers for the Holy Qurbana (CCC 2174).

qa: Why does Mark end with fear and silence?

Many scholars think Mark ended deliberately at v. 8, leaving the reader to answer the message the women first received in trembling: he is going ahead of you. Others think the original ending was lost. Either way the Church has received the longer ending (16:9–20) as part of Scripture, and Mark himself has already told us, through Jesus' own predictions, that the disciples will see him (14:28; 16:7).
Mark says the women came “when the sun had risen”. Do the Gospels disagree about the time?

The Gospels describe the same morning from different angles: “at early dawn” (Luke 24:1), “while it was still dark” (John 20:1), “very early … when the sun had risen” (Mark 16:2). The women set out in the dark and arrived as the day broke. The details differ; the testimony is one.
rite: In Syriac the first day of the week is called ḥad b-šabbā, “the first in the week”. Every Sunday is for us a little feast of the Resurrection. Our tradition loves the image of the East: the rising sun is a sign of the risen Lord, whose coming in glory will be like the lightning that “comes from the east” (Matthew 24:27). Tomorrow, New Sunday, closes the first week of the Resurrection with the confession of Mar Thoma. Today's epistle gives the attitude for that feast: hearts set where Christ is.
study: The women set out not knowing who would roll away the stone. What act of love am I putting off because I cannot see how the obstacle will be removed?
“And Peter”: whom do I need to name and include in the good news, even after a failure?
What would it mean, in the week ahead, to “seek the things that are above” in my work and family?

lead: New Sunday closes the first week of the Resurrection, and for the Syro-Malabar Church it is the feast of the faith of Mar Thoma. A week after Easter the risen Lord comes again through locked doors and leads Thomas to the confession “My Lord and my God!”. Isaiah promises a word that will not return empty and nations that will run to God's people. Acts shows the first fruit of the Resurrection: a community of one heart and soul, where the apostles bear witness with great power and no one is in need. Colossians sings who the risen one is: the image of the invisible God, the firstborn from the dead, in whom all things hold together. The readings move from God's word, through the community it creates, to the Lord himself confessed as God. The key words are witness, peace and believe.

r.h: My word shall not return to me empty
set: This is the last chapter of the part of Isaiah addressed to the exiles in Babylon. It opens with an invitation to a banquet: “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters” (55:1). God promises “an everlasting covenant, my steadfast, sure love for David” (55:3). The promise once made to David's house is now opened to the whole people.

St Paul, preaching at Antioch in Pisidia, quotes v. 3 as fulfilled in the Resurrection: God raised Jesus from the dead, “no more to return to corruption”, and so gave “the holy promises made to David” (Acts 13:34). That is one reason this chapter is read in the season of the Resurrection.
str: vv. 4–5: David a witness to the peoples; the nations will run to you.
vv. 6–7: seek the Lord; let the wicked return; he will pardon.
vv. 8–9: God's thoughts and ways are higher.
vv. 10–11: rain and snow; the word that accomplishes its purpose.
vv. 12–13: going out in joy; creation sings; the myrtle in place of the brier.
kw: David was a witness to the nations of what God had done for Israel. The New Testament gives the same task to the apostles: “you will be my witnesses … to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

The great word of conversion in the prophets. The wicked are to “return to the Lord” (v. 7), and God's word does not “return” to him empty (v. 11). Our return to God is the fruit of his word coming to us.
In Hebrew a word is also a deed. God's word is not a sound that fades: it goes out, does its work and comes back fulfilled.
vv: See, I made him a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples.
Seek the Lord while he may be found, call upon him while he is near;
Urgency and tenderness together. God is near now; the time to seek him is now.
For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord.
In context this is first about mercy: God pardons more abundantly than we would (v. 7). His ways are higher above all in forgiving.
so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose,

Christians hear in this the Word who came from the Father and returned to him with his work accomplished: “I came from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and am going to the Father” (John 16:28).
Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle;
Thorns and thistles were the sign of the curse in Genesis 3:18. Here the curse is reversed, and the earth itself shares in the joy of the redeemed.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that such is the force and power of the word of God that it is the support and energy of the Church, the strength of faith for her children and the food of the soul (Dei Verbum 21, in substance). Today's Gospel shows that power at work: Thomas comes to faith because the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord,” and because the Lord himself spoke to him. Today, says the Gospel, others will believe through the word without seeing (John 20:29, 31).

set: This is the second of three summaries in which Luke describes the life of the Jerusalem community (2:42–47; 4:32–35; 5:12–16). It comes just after the apostles have been released by the council and the community has prayed so that the place shook (4:23–31). The common life is the fruit of the Resurrection and of the Spirit.

The sharing was not imposed by law. When Ananias and Sapphira lie about their gift, Peter reminds them that the land was theirs and the money was at their disposal (5:4). Their sin was the lie, not keeping their property.
str: v. 32: one heart and soul; possessions held in common.
v. 33: the apostles' powerful witness to the Resurrection.
vv. 34–35: no one in need; goods distributed according to need.
vv. 36–37: the example of Barnabas.
kw: A common expression for deep friendship among the Greeks, and a Hebrew way of speaking of the whole person. Luke shows that the risen Lord has made of many believers one person.

The same word as in 2:44. Luke may also be echoing God's promise to Israel: “There will, however, be no one in need among you” (Deuteronomy 15:4). The Resurrection community lives what the Law hoped for.
Luke gives the name the meaning “son of encouragement”. Barnabas will later stand beside the newly converted Saul when others were afraid of him (9:27) and will go with him on mission.
vv: Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul,
With great power the apostles gave their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
The common life is set around the witness to the Resurrection. The sharing is not a programme on its own; it flows from faith in the risen Lord.
There was not a needy person among them,
He sold a field that belonged to him, then brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
To lay a gift at someone's feet was a sign of handing it over completely. The gift goes through the apostles, so it is shared by the whole Church and not given as a private favour.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of the communion of saints, recalls that the first believers “had everything in common” and that what the true Christian has is to be regarded as a good possessed in common with everyone else (CCC 952, in substance). St Augustine opened his Rule for those living together in community with this verse: to live in harmony, with one mind and one heart on the way to God (in substance). Religious life in every age has looked to this passage, and every parish is called to its spirit of sharing.

set: After the greeting and a prayer of thanksgiving, the letter sings a hymn to Christ (vv. 15–20). Many scholars think it was an early Christian hymn that the author took up. It has two strophes: Christ and creation (vv. 15–17), and Christ and the new creation, the Church and reconciliation (vv. 18–20). The word “firstborn” stands in each.
The hymn answers those at Colossae who feared other powers. Whatever “thrones or dominions or rulers or powers” there may be, all were created through Christ and for him (v. 16).
str: vv. 12–14: thanks to the Father, who has moved us from darkness into the kingdom of his Son.
vv. 15–17: Christ, the image of God, firstborn of all creation; all things created in him and held together in him.
v. 18: head of the body, the Church; firstborn from the dead.
vv. 19–20: all the fullness dwells in him; peace through the blood of his Cross.
kw: The invisible God becomes visible in Christ. Humanity was made in God's image (Genesis 1:27); Christ is the image. “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

In Scripture the firstborn has first place and the inheritance. The word does not mean that Christ is the first creature. St Athanasius answered the Arians that the Son is called firstborn not because he was made, but because he came down to his creatures and became the first to rise from the dead (in substance). The Creed says, “begotten, not made”.
To change enemies into friends. The reconciliation reaches “all things, whether on earth or in heaven”, and it is made at the price of “the blood of his cross”.
vv: He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son,
The language of a new Exodus. The baptized have changed kingdoms.
He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation;
He himself is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
Christ is not only the beginning of creation but also what holds it together now. Nothing falls apart that is held in him.
He is the head of the body, the church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead,
The Resurrection makes him the first of a new creation. On New Sunday the Church hears that the one Thomas touched is the head of the body to which we belong.
and through him God was pleased to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, by making peace through the blood of his cross.
The wounds Thomas is invited to touch are the price of this peace.
ch: The Catechism quotes this hymn to teach that God created everything by the eternal Word, his beloved Son: in him all things were created, and in him all things hold together (CCC 291). It quotes v. 18 when it speaks of Christ as head of the Church, his body (CCC 792). The faith of Nicaea, that the Son is “begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father”, is the Church's reading of this hymn: the one who is firstborn is the eternal Son, through whom all things were made.

set: It is the evening of the first day of the week. Mary Magdalene has told the disciples, “I have seen the Lord” (20:18), yet they are behind locked doors. John says they were afraid “of the Jews”. In John's Gospel this phrase often means the authorities in Jerusalem who had opposed Jesus (compare 7:13; 9:22). The disciples themselves were Jews, and so was Jesus. It is no accusation against the Jewish people.

The passage has two scenes, a week apart. Thomas is absent from the first, refuses to believe the testimony of the others, and is present at the second. The Gospel's first ending follows at once: these things are written “so that you may come to believe” (20:31).
str: vv. 19–20: Jesus comes; “Peace be with you”; he shows his hands and side; joy.
vv. 21–23: the sending, the breath of the Spirit, the power to forgive and retain sins.
vv. 24–25: Thomas absent; “Unless I see …”.
vv. 26–27: a week later; Jesus invites Thomas to touch.
vv. 28–29: Thomas's confession; the blessing of those who believe without seeing.
kw: The ordinary Hebrew greeting, šālôm, but now spoken by the one who promised, “my peace I give to you” (14:27). He says it three times in this passage. To men who had abandoned him, his first word is peace, not reproach.
The Greek Old Testament uses this verb in Genesis 2:7, when God breathed into the first man the breath of life. The risen Lord breathes the Holy Spirit, and a new creation begins.
The Greek translation of his Aramaic name, Thomas, which means “twin”. The same Thomas had said, when Jesus went toward Jerusalem, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (11:16).
ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou
The highest confession of faith in the Gospels. John's Gospel began, “the Word was God” (1:1), and near its end a disciple says it to Jesus himself.
vv: Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”
As the Father has sent me, so I send you.
The mission of the Church is the mission of the Son, continued.
If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.
The first gift of the risen Lord through the Spirit is the power to forgive. The Church sees here the institution of the sacrament of reconciliation (CCC 1485).
Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.
Jesus offers Thomas exactly what he had demanded. The risen body still bears its wounds. John does not say that Thomas touched them; the invitation was enough.
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.
This is the last beatitude in the Gospels, and it is spoken for us.
ch: The Catechism notes that at the appearance of the risen Jesus the title “Lord” becomes adoration: “My Lord and my God!” (CCC 448). It teaches that on Easter evening the Lord gave the apostles his own power to forgive sins (CCC 976; 1485), and the Council of Trent taught that these words refer to the power of forgiving and retaining sins in the sacrament of Penance. St Gregory the Great said in a homily that the unbelief of Thomas did more for our faith than the faith of the disciples who believed: his doubt was healed, and our doubt is healed with his (in substance).

qa: Was Thomas wrong to doubt?

He was slow to believe the witness of his brothers, and Jesus gently rebukes that: “Do not doubt but believe.” But his doubt was not a rejection of Jesus. He stayed with the community, he was there the next Sunday, and when the Lord came, he made the greatest confession in the Gospels. His story shows that honest struggle, held within the Church, can end in deep faith.
Did the first Christians abolish private property (Acts 4:32)?

No. Their sharing was willing, as Peter's words in 5:4 show. The Church has always taught both the right to private property and that goods are meant for all, so that property must serve the common good and the poor (CCC 2402–2406).
What does it mean that Christ is the “firstborn of all creation”?

It means that he has first place over all creation, not that he was the first thing God made. The same hymn says that all things were created in him and through him, so he cannot himself be one of the things created. The Church confesses him as the eternal Son, “begotten, not made”.
rite: For the Syro-Malabar Church, New Sunday (Puthu Njayar) is a feast of family. We are the Mar Thoma Christians, and today's Gospel tells the faith of our father. According to our tradition, Mar Thoma Shliha came to Kerala in AD 52, founded communities, and was martyred at Mylapore. His confession, “My Lord and my God”, is on the lips of many of our faithful at the elevation of the Holy Qurbana. On this day many go on pilgrimage to the hill shrine of Malayattoor, linked by our tradition to the apostle's prayer. The name “New Sunday” also recalls the newness of the Resurrection: the first Sunday after the feast, when the Church begins again to live the new life given at Easter.
study: Thomas came to faith in the community, on the next Sunday. What helps me to stay with the Church when my faith is struggling?
Jesus' first word to those who abandoned him was “Peace.” To whom do I need to bring that first word?
Acts says there was no one in need among them. Who is in need in my parish, and what can I share?
When I say or hear “My Lord and my God” at the Holy Qurbana, what do I mean by it?

lead: Both readings are about recognizing the one Lord. Paul pleads with the Corinthians not to split into parties around their preachers, because Christ is not divided and it was not Paul who was crucified for them. At Emmaus two disciples recognize the risen Jesus in the breaking of the bread and run back to the community in Jerusalem. The Lord is known at the table, and he gathers those who were scattered.

set: Paul founded the Church at Corinth, a busy port city of Greece, around AD 50–51, and wrote this letter a few years later from Ephesus (16:8). He has heard from “Chloe's people”, probably members of her household, that the community is breaking into groups, each attached to a favourite teacher. This is the first problem he takes up, and it shapes the whole letter.
str: v. 10: the appeal for unity.
vv. 11–12: the report and the slogans.
vv. 13–16: three questions, and Paul's thanks that he baptized so few.
v. 17: his mission: to preach the Cross.
kw: Literally “tears”, as in a torn garment. It is the root of our word schism. Paul is not speaking yet of separate Churches but of factions inside one community.
The verb means to mend or restore. Mark uses it of James and John mending their nets (Mark 1:19). Unity is something to be repaired with patience, like a net, so that it can hold.
The Aramaic name of Peter, meaning “rock”. Paul uses it often. Apollos was an eloquent Jewish Christian from Alexandria who taught at Corinth after Paul (Acts 18:24–28).
vv: Now I appeal to you, brothers and sisters, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you be in agreement and that there be no divisions among you,
Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
Each question expects the answer no. The Church belongs to the one who died for her, not to the one who preached to her.
For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the gospel, and not with eloquent wisdom, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied of its power.

Paul does not make light of Baptism; he has just said that they were baptized into Christ's name. He means that his own task was to preach, and that the power is in the Cross, not in the preacher's skill.
ch: The Second Vatican Council begins its decree on ecumenism by saying that Christ founded one Church, and that division openly contradicts his will, is a scandal to the world and harms the preaching of the Gospel (Unitatis Redintegratio 1). Paul's questions still speak to every parish and diocese: whenever we gather around a person rather than around Christ, the Body is torn.

r.h: Known in the breaking of the bread
set: On the day of the Resurrection two disciples, one named Cleopas, are walking from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, sad and confused. A stranger joins them and explains the Scriptures about the Messiah (24:13–27). As evening falls they reach the village. This reading tells what happened at the table and afterwards.
str: vv. 28–29: he seems to go on; they urge him to stay.
vv. 30–31: at table he takes, blesses, breaks and gives; their eyes are opened; he vanishes.
v. 32: their hearts were burning.
vv. 33–35: they return to Jerusalem; the Lord has appeared to Simon; they tell their story.
kw: The same verb that John uses for abiding. The disciples' prayer, “Stay with us”, has become one of the Church's best-loved prayers at evening.
The phrase the first Christians used for the Eucharist (Acts 2:42). Luke's four verbs, took, blessed, broke and gave, are the verbs of the feeding of the crowd (9:16) and of the Last Supper (22:19).
vv: But they urged him strongly, saying, “Stay with us, because it is almost evening and the day is now nearly over.” So he went in to stay with them.
He does not force his company on them. He waits to be invited.
When he was at the table with them, he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them.
The guest becomes the host.
Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.
The story moves in the same order as the Holy Qurbana: first the Scriptures opened, then the bread broken, then the mission.
ch: The Catechism lists “the breaking of bread” among the names of the Eucharist, the name by which the first Christians called their gatherings, and it points to Emmaus (CCC 1329). It describes the Eucharistic celebration as following the same movement as the paschal meal of the risen Jesus with his disciples: he walked with them, explained the Scriptures, and broke the bread (CCC 1347).

qa: Does Paul make light of Baptism when he thanks God that he baptized few?

No. He is thankful only because no one can now claim to belong to Paul's party. In the same letter he teaches that “in the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (12:13). Baptism unites us to Christ, not to the minister who baptizes.
study: Around whom or what do I sometimes gather, instead of around Christ? What helps me mend the net of unity in my parish?
The disciples recognized Jesus only at the table. How can I prepare my heart so that I recognize him at the Holy Qurbana?

lead: Both readings ask who Jesus is and where the evidence for him lies. In Damascus, Saul, newly converted, proves from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Messiah and proclaims him as the Son of God, and soon he must escape by night in a basket. In John, Jesus tells those who opposed him that Moses himself wrote about him. The Scriptures of Israel, rightly read, lead to Christ.

r.h: He is the Son of God
set: Saul had come to Damascus with letters from the high priest to arrest believers (9:1–2). On the road the risen Lord met him, and Ananias baptized him (9:3–19). Now, “immediately”, the persecutor becomes a preacher in the same synagogues where he meant to make arrests.

Paul gives his own account in his letters. He went away into Arabia and returned to Damascus (Galatians 1:17), and he tells of being let down in a basket through a window in the wall when the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city to seize him (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). The “some time” of v. 23 may include the stay in Arabia.
str: v. 20: Saul proclaims Jesus as Son of God in the synagogues.
v. 21: amazement: is this not the persecutor?
v. 22: he grows stronger and proves that Jesus is the Messiah.
vv. 23–25: the plot; the watch on the gates; the escape in a basket.
kw: A rare title in Acts. Saul's first preaching goes to the centre of the faith he had fought against: Jesus is not only a teacher or prophet but the Son.
Literally “bringing together”. Saul places the Scriptures side by side with what happened to Jesus and shows that they fit.
vv: and immediately he began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.”
Saul became increasingly more powerful and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Messiah.
The debate takes place among Jews, about the meaning of Israel's own Scriptures. Saul himself is a Jew and remains proud of it (Philippians 3:5).
but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
The great apostle begins his ministry in a humble way, hidden in a basket. Paul himself lists it among the things he boasts of, his weaknesses (2 Corinthians 11:30–33).
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it teaches that the confession of Christ's divine sonship stood at the centre of the apostolic faith from the beginning: Paul, to whom the Father revealed his Son, at once proclaimed in the synagogues, “He is the Son of God” (CCC 442). The story also shows the Church's confidence in God's grace: the man who came to bind believers is now carried to safety by them.

set: After Jesus healed a man at the pool of Bethesda on a sabbath (5:1–9), some of the authorities in Jerusalem began to oppose him, and John says they sought to kill him because he called God his own Father (5:16–18). Jesus answers with a long discourse. In its last part he names his witnesses: John the Baptist, his own works, the Father, and the Scriptures (5:31–40). These closing verses are spoken to those opponents, not to the Jewish people as a whole.
str: vv. 41–42: Jesus does not seek human glory.
vv. 43–44: they receive one who comes in his own name, not the one who comes in the Father's name.
vv. 45–47: Moses, in whom they hope, will be their accuser, for he wrote about Jesus.
kw: In John, glory is the weight of honour. The problem is not a lack of learning but of desire: those who seek honour from one another cannot receive the honour that comes from God alone.
Moses was the great intercessor for Israel (Exodus 32:11–14). Jesus says that the one they trust to speak for them will speak against their unbelief, because his writings point to Jesus.
vv: I do not accept glory from human beings.
How can you believe when you accept glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the one who alone is God?
Faith is blocked less by hard questions than by the wish to be admired. To believe, a person must care more for what God thinks than for what others think.
If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.
Christians have read this especially of Moses' promise, “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me” (Deuteronomy 18:15).
ch: The Church reads the Old Testament in the light of Christ, while keeping its own lasting value. The Second Vatican Council, quoting St Augustine, says that the New Testament is hidden in the Old and the Old is made manifest in the New (Dei Verbum 16; CCC 129). Jesus' words are no rejection of Moses. They are an invitation to read Moses to the end, where he leads.

qa: Acts says “the Jews plotted to kill him” (9:23). How should we read this?

Luke means some Jewish opponents in Damascus at that time, not the Jewish people. Paul himself says that the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city (2 Corinthians 11:32), so others were involved too. Saul, the disciples who saved him and the first Church were also Jews. The Church firmly rejects any blame of the Jewish people as a whole (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
study: Saul preached “immediately”. Is there a grace I have received that I have been slow to share?
Jesus says that seeking glory from one another blocks faith. Whose approval matters most to me in my daily choices?

lead: In the season of the Resurrection the Church thinks of those who have just been baptized and of all of us who were raised with Christ in baptism. Paul tells the Galatians that Christ has released them from slavery, and that what counts is “faith working through love”. In the Gospel Jesus opens the ears and loosens the tongue of a man who could not hear or speak well. Freedom in Paul and opening in Mark are one gift: the risen Lord releases what was bound so that we can hear his word and speak his praise. The words to watch are freedom, yoke and Ephphatha.

r.h: For freedom Christ has set us free
set: Paul had brought the Gospel to the Galatians, Gentiles in central Asia Minor. After he left, other teachers came and told them that to belong fully to God’s people they must also be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. For Paul this was not a small matter of custom. If a Gentile is told that circumcision is needed in order to be justified, then Christ alone is no longer enough. Chapters 3–4 have argued this from Abraham and from the two sons of Abraham; today’s verses draw the conclusion.

Paul is not attacking the Jewish people or Jewish practice. He was a Jew himself, and he speaks here to Gentile believers about what is required of them. His point is that righteousness comes by God’s grace in Christ, received in faith, and not by taking on the Law as a condition.
str: v. 1: the thesis: “For freedom Christ has set us free”; stand firm.
vv. 2–4: a solemn warning: to seek justification by the Law is to be cut off from Christ.
v. 5: the Christian way of waiting: by the Spirit, through faith, in hope.
v. 6: what really counts: faith working through love.
kw: Not the right to do anything at all, but release from slavery into sonship. A few verses later Paul adds: “do not use your freedom as an opportunity for self-indulgence, but through love become slaves to one another” (5:13).

The wooden beam on the neck of an ox. Jewish teachers could speak warmly of the “yoke of the Law” as a joyful service. Paul uses the image for anything that would put a believer back under slavery, and Jesus offers his own yoke as easy (Matthew 11:29–30).
The word from which “energy” comes. Faith is not idle. It is alive and at work, and its working is love.
vv: For freedom Christ has set us free. Stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
The freedom is already given. Paul does not tell them to win it, but to “stand firm” in what they have received.
You who want to be justified by the law have cut yourselves off from Christ; you have fallen away from grace.
Strong words. To make anything else the ground of our justification is to step away from grace, which is the only ground.
the only thing that counts is faith working through love.
This is one of the clearest lines in Paul on faith and love together. Faith that saves is not a bare opinion; it is faith that loves. By grace, love is the very life of faith.
ch: The Council of Trent took up this verse when it taught that in justification faith is joined with hope and charity, since faith without them does not unite a person perfectly with Christ (Decree on Justification, chapter 7, in substance). Catholics and Lutherans, in their Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), were able to say together that we are accepted by God by grace alone, through faith in Christ, and not because of any merit of ours, and that this grace renews the heart and moves us to good works. Our good works are themselves the fruit of grace.

set: Jesus has been in the region of Tyre, where he healed the daughter of a Gentile woman (7:24–30). Now he takes a long road: north to Sidon and then down to the east side of the Sea of Galilee, into the Decapolis, the “ten cities”, a largely Gentile region. Earlier, the people of this same region had begged him to leave (5:17). Now they bring a man to him.
Mark keeps the Aramaic word that Jesus spoke, Ephphatha. It is one of the few places where the Gospels let us hear the Lord’s own language, the sister tongue of our Syriac.
str: vv. 31–32: the journey; a deaf man with a speech impediment is brought.
vv. 33–34: Jesus takes him aside, touches ears and tongue, looks up, sighs, and speaks.
v. 35: the healing.
vv. 36–37: the command to silence, and the crowd’s astonished praise.
kw: with an impediment in his speech

A very rare Greek word. In the Greek Old Testament it appears only in Isaiah 35:6, “the tongue of the speechless sing for joy”, in a promise of the day when God comes to save. Mark is hinting that this day has come.
Aramaic, which Mark translates for his readers. The command is spoken to the man, not only to his ears: the whole person is opened.
A deep groan. Jesus does not heal from a distance or without feeling. Paul uses the same family of words for creation and the Spirit groaning for redemption (Romans 8:22–26).
vv: He took him aside in private, away from the crowd, and put his fingers into his ears, and he spat and touched his tongue.
The healing begins with a meeting apart. The man cannot hear words, so Jesus speaks to him by touch, in a language he can understand.
Then looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.”
He looks to the Father before he speaks. The healing comes from the communion between the Son and the Father.
He has done everything well; he even makes the deaf to hear and the mute to speak.
Many readers hear an echo of creation, when God saw that everything he had made was very good (Genesis 1:31), and of Isaiah 35:5–6. In Jesus, God is making things new.
ch: Very early this healing was joined to baptism. St Ambrose explained to the newly baptized in Milan the rite called “Ephphatha”, in which the bishop touched their ears and nostrils before baptism, so that they might be opened to the word and to the fragrance of Christ (On the Mysteries, in substance). The Church sees in this man every believer whom Christ opens to hear the Gospel and to confess the faith. Those who have received the Word must also speak it: the crowd in the Decapolis could not keep silent.

qa: Why does Jesus tell them to tell no one, and why do they disobey?

Mark often shows Jesus asking for silence about his miracles. He did not want to be taken for a mere wonder-worker; who he is would be fully seen only on the Cross and in the Resurrection. The people cannot hold back their joy. Now that he is risen, the command is the opposite: go and proclaim it (Mark 16:15).
study: Paul says, “Stand firm” in the freedom Christ has given. What old yoke do I keep picking up again?
Jesus took the man aside before he healed him. Where could I go apart with the Lord this week, so that he can open my ears and loosen my tongue?

lead: Both readings are about faith that holds on under pressure. Paul, writing from prison, tells the Philippians that it is a gift of grace not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him. In the Gospel a Gentile mother will not stop asking, even when Jesus seems to refuse her, and he praises her: “Woman, great is your faith!” The risen Lord does not promise an easy road, but he gives a faith that does not let go. The words to watch are worthy, granted and crumbs.

r.h: Not only believing, but suffering for him
set: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison (1:13), not knowing whether he will live or die (1:20–24). Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, proud of its citizenship. It was the first city in Europe where Paul preached, and there he and Silas were beaten and thrown into prison (Acts 16:19–24). The believers had seen his struggle with their own eyes. Now they face opposition of their own.
str: v. 27: live as citizens worthy of the Gospel, standing firm and striving together.
v. 28: do not be frightened by opponents; God is at work.
vv. 29–30: suffering for Christ is a gift, and they share Paul’s own struggle.
kw: Literally “live as citizens”. In a city proud of its Roman rights, Paul reminds them of another citizenship: “our citizenship is in heaven” (3:20).
A word from the games: athletes struggling together as a team. The Christian life is not a solo race.
From the same root as charis, grace. Suffering for Christ is counted among the gifts of grace, not as a punishment.
vv: Only, live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ
Paul does not first say “believe the right things”, but “live worthily”. The Gospel is meant to be seen in the way the community lives.
and are in no way intimidated by your opponents.
The Greek word was used of a horse that shies in fright. Courage here is not a natural temperament but a fruit of trust that “this is God’s doing”.
For he has graciously granted you the privilege not only of believing in Christ, but of suffering for him as well
Faith itself is a gift; so is the strength to suffer with Christ. Paul does not seek suffering for its own sake. He sees that a disciple shares the road of the Master.
ch: The Church honours the martyrs as those who bore the highest witness to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). Paul’s words also console all who suffer in many lands for the name of Christ today. The Church prays for them, and for those who wrong them, as Jesus taught (Matthew 5:44).

set: Jesus goes into the region of Tyre and Sidon, Gentile cities on the coast north of Galilee. Mark calls the woman “a Gentile, of Syrophoenician origin” (Mark 7:26). Matthew calls her “a Canaanite”, an old name that recalls the peoples who lived in the land before Israel. In Matthew’s Gospel Jesus has already sent the Twelve only to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:5–6). After the Resurrection he will send the apostles to all nations (28:19). This woman stands between those two moments.
str: vv. 21–22: the woman cries out for her daughter.
v. 23: Jesus is silent; the disciples want her sent away.
v. 24: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
vv. 25–27: she kneels, asks again, and answers his saying about the dogs.
v. 28: Jesus praises her faith, and her daughter is healed.
kw: The cry of the needy in the Gospels, and the cry the Church has never stopped praying: Kyrie eleison, Lord, have mercy.
A diminutive: the little dogs of the house, under the table. The saying is still hard, and the woman does not deny it. She takes it up and finds room in it for herself.
Only two people in Matthew are praised for a faith so great, and both are Gentiles: this woman and the centurion (8:10).
vv: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is tormented by a demon.
A Gentile woman calls Jesus by a title of Israel’s Messiah. She also makes her daughter’s pain her own: “have mercy on me”.
But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.”
The shortest prayer in the passage, and perhaps the most complete. Silence and refusal do not stop her; they bring her closer.
Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.
She does not argue against Jesus; she agrees with him, and then trusts that his table is so rich that even the crumbs are enough.
Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.
ch: St John Chrysostom says that Jesus delayed his answer not to hurt the woman but to bring her faith into the light, so that all could see what was hidden in her (Homilies on Matthew, in substance). The Church has always loved her humble persistence as a model of prayer. The Catechism teaches that Jesus hears the prayer of faith, and among its examples is the Canaanite woman who asks for her daughter (CCC 2616). Her words about the crumbs can teach us how to come to the Holy Qurbana: we come not because we deserve the table, but because the Lord is generous.

qa: Was Jesus being harsh to the woman?

His words sound hard, and Matthew does not soften them. But the story moves from silence to praise. Jesus draws out a faith that the disciples, who wanted her sent away, did not see. Her daughter is healed, and the woman is held up for all generations as a model. The story also shows the order of God’s plan: first to Israel, then through Israel to the nations.
study: Paul calls suffering for Christ a gift of grace. Is there a hardship in my life that I could offer to the Lord in this light?
The woman kept asking when the answer seemed to be no. For whom do I need to keep praying with her persistence?

lead: On a Friday of the Resurrection season the Church still looks at the Cross, now with Easter eyes. Paul says that the message of the Cross looks like foolishness, yet it is the power and wisdom of God. In the Gospel Jesus tells of a sower whose seed seems to be wasted on path, rock and thorns, and yet the harvest is beyond all expectation. Both readings teach the same patience of God: what looks weak and lost is where his power is at work. The words to watch are foolishness, power and listen.

set: Corinth was a rich and busy port city in Greece, where public speakers and teachers of wisdom were admired. The Christians there had begun to divide into groups, each attached to a favourite preacher: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos” (1:12). Paul answers by going to the centre: the Gospel is not one more school of clever speech. Its heart is a crucified Messiah, and that turns the world’s measure of wisdom upside down.
str: v. 18: the thesis: the word of the Cross is foolishness to some, the power of God to others.
vv. 19–20: Scripture and three questions: where are the wise?
v. 21: God chose to save believers through the “foolishness” of preaching.
vv. 22–24: signs, wisdom, and Christ crucified, the power and wisdom of God.
kw: Literally “the word of the cross”. Paul does not preach a theory about the Cross; he proclaims a person who was crucified.
Related to the word from which “moron” comes. To a cultured ear in Corinth, a crucified saviour sounded absurd: crucifixion was the death of slaves and rebels.

A trap or an obstacle on the road. For many devout Jews of Paul’s day, a Messiah who died under a curse (see Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13) was hard to accept. Paul, himself a Jew, had once stumbled at it.
vv: For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
Note the tenses: “being saved” is a road we are on. Salvation has begun and is still going on in us.
For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
Paul quotes Isaiah 29:14 largely in its Greek form. God has always overturned human pride.
but we proclaim Christ crucified

Not a successful hero, not a clever argument, but “Christ crucified”. The Greek participle suggests one who was crucified and remains the Crucified, even in his risen glory, as the risen Lord still bears his wounds.
but to those who are the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
God’s call crosses every line. The first believers were Jews, and Gentiles were added to them.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God showed his almighty power above all in the voluntary humiliation and Resurrection of his Son, and quotes the verse that follows today’s reading: the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men (CCC 272). The Church does not hide the Cross after Easter. In the East Syriac tradition the Cross is honoured as the sign of victory and of the Lord’s glorious return; the risen Lord is the Crucified who conquered.

r.h: A sower went out to sow
set: This is the first long parable in Mark’s Gospel. Jesus teaches from a boat on the Sea of Galilee, with the crowd on the shore. Mark has already shown that some people are opposed to Jesus, others are confused, and some follow him (chapters 2–3). The parable speaks to that situation: why does the word bear fruit in some hearts and not in others? The explanation of the parable comes in vv. 13–20, which are not part of today’s reading.
str: vv. 1–2: the setting: a boat, a crowd, teaching in parables.
v. 3: “Listen!” A sower goes out.
vv. 4–7: three losses: the path, the rocky ground, the thorns.
v. 8: the good soil and the great harvest.
v. 9: “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
kw: In the background is the Hebrew mashal: a comparison, a riddle, a story that makes the listener think. A parable does not explain everything; it invites.
The parable begins and ends with a call to hear. Every devout Jew prayed daily, “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Hearing in the Bible means receiving and obeying.
An extraordinary harvest. When Isaac reaped a hundredfold, it was a sign of God’s blessing (Genesis 26:12). The point is not farming skill, but the abundance of God’s kingdom.
vv: “Listen! A sower went out to sow.
The sower is generous, even careless by human standards. He scatters seed everywhere. God does not hold back his word from anyone.
And when the sun rose, it was scorched; and since it had no root, it withered away.
Quick enthusiasm without roots does not last. The heat that should help the plant grow destroys it.
Other seed fell into good soil and brought forth grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.
Three failures, but the story ends in a harvest that more than makes up for every loss. That is the hope of the parable.
ch: The Catechism says that the parables are like mirrors for us: will we be hard soil or good earth? Jesus asks for a decision, and to know the secrets of the kingdom one must become his disciple (CCC 546). The Second Vatican Council compares the word of God to a seed sown in a field: those who hear it with faith and are joined to the little flock of Christ have received the kingdom itself (Lumen Gentium 5, in substance).

qa: Why does the sower waste so much seed?

The parable is not a lesson in efficient farming. It shows God’s generosity: he sows his word in every heart, even where it seems useless. He does not first choose the good soil and ignore the rest. Our task is to become good soil, and to sow as generously as he does.
study: Where in my life does the Cross still look like foolishness to me, and where have I seen it as the power of God?
Which of the four soils best describes how I received God’s word this week? What would help it take root?

lead: The risen Lord stands among his frightened disciples and says, “Peace be with you.” Paul, writing to the Colossians, prays that this peace of Christ may rule in their hearts, and that the word of Christ may dwell in them richly as they sing and give thanks. The Gospel shows that the peace is not an idea but a person: Jesus with real hands and feet, who eats before them. The words to watch are peace, thankful and flesh and bones.

r.h: Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley in Asia Minor. The letter tells the believers that they have been raised with Christ and must now “seek the things that are above” (3:1). Paul then describes the new life as a change of clothes: take off the old self, put on the new (3:9–12). Today’s verses are the crowning garment and what follows from it.
