Many scholars think that Colossians was written by a disciple of Paul in his name; others hold that Paul wrote it himself, perhaps with a co-worker. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.
str: v. 14: above all, love, which binds everything together.
v. 15: the peace of Christ as the umpire of the heart; be thankful.
v. 16: the word of Christ dwelling richly; teaching and singing.
v. 17: do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks.
kw: Love is the belt that holds all the other virtues in place, so that together they make one whole. Without love the other virtues fall apart.
A word from the games: the umpire who decides. When the heart is divided, the peace of Christ is to give the decision.
Thanks is named three times in these four verses (vv. 15, 16, 17). The Greek word is the root of “Eucharist”, the great thanksgiving of the Church.
vv: Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
The Greek has no new verb here; “clothe yourselves” carries on from v. 12. Love is the last and outer garment that holds the rest together.
And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in the one body. And be thankful.
This peace is not only inner calm. We are called to it “in the one body”, the Church; it is peace among brothers and sisters.
with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God.
Singing is one of the ways the word of Christ lives in a community. The early Church prayed the psalms and also composed new hymns to Christ.
And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is above all thanksgiving to the Father, a blessing by which the Church expresses her gratitude for all his benefits (CCC 1359–1360). Paul’s words also describe the Church’s prayer: the word, the psalms, the hymns and thanksgiving all meet in the Liturgy. In the Holy Qurbana the priest greets the people more than once with the risen Lord’s own words, “Peace be with you”, so that his peace may rule among us.

r.h: See that it is I myself
set: It is still Easter Sunday evening in Luke’s account. The two disciples have returned from Emmaus and are telling how they knew the Lord in the breaking of the bread (24:35). The eleven and those with them have just said, “The Lord has risen indeed, and he has appeared to Simon!” (24:34). And while they are talking, he is there.
str: v. 36: Jesus stands among them: “Peace be with you.”
vv. 37–38: fear: they think they see a ghost.
vv. 39–40: hands and feet: “Touch me and see.”
vv. 41–43: joy mixed with disbelief; Jesus eats a piece of fish.
kw: The everyday greeting shalom, now spoken by one who has passed through death. In the risen Lord’s mouth it is the gift of reconciliation.
The disciples think they are seeing a spirit without a body. Jesus corrects them: the Resurrection is not a vision or a ghost story.
Jesus insists on the reality of his body. It is the same body that was crucified, now glorified.
vv: While they were talking about this, Jesus himself stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”
A few ancient manuscripts lack the words “and said to them, ‘Peace be with you’”, but almost all have them, and they match John 20:19.
Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.
The wounds show who he is. The risen Lord does not leave behind his Passion; he carries it into glory.
While in their joy they were disbelieving and still wondering
An honest line. Joy can be so great that it is hard to believe. Faith grows slowly, and the Lord is patient with it.
and he took it and ate in their presence.
He does not need food; he eats for them, to show that he is truly alive. Peter later preaches that the apostles “ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the risen Jesus showed the disciples that he was not a ghost, invited them to touch him, and ate with them, and that his body is the same body that suffered and died, now risen with new properties (CCC 645). Christ rose with his own body, and so shall we (CCC 999). St Ignatius of Antioch, writing on his way to martyrdom, defends this against those who said the Lord only seemed to have a body: he was in the flesh even after the Resurrection, and the apostles touched him and believed (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 3, in substance).

qa: If his body was real, how could he suddenly stand among them, or come in through locked doors (John 20:19)?

The risen body of Jesus is real, but it is no longer bound by space and time in the way our bodies are. It is a glorified body, sharing in the life of the Spirit. It is not a return to earthly life, as with Lazarus (CCC 645–646). This is why the disciples sometimes did not recognize him at first, and why he could come and go as he willed.
study: Paul says that the peace of Christ should be the umpire in my heart. Which decision before me now needs that umpire?
Jesus showed his wounds to frightened friends. How can my own healed wounds help someone else to believe?

lead: Today’s readings open doors. Isaiah promises that foreigners and eunuchs, who feared they had no place among God’s people, will be brought to his holy mountain, because his house is “a house of prayer for all peoples”. In Acts the wise teacher Gamaliel advises the council to let the apostles alone, and the apostles go out rejoicing and keep proclaiming Jesus as the Messiah, in the Temple and at home. Ephesians sings the blessing of the Father who chose us, the Son who redeemed us, and the Spirit who seals us. In the Gospel Jesus tells his troubled friends that in his Father’s house there is room, and that he himself is the way there. The readings move from a promise of welcome, through witness under pressure and a hymn of blessing, to the Way who leads us home. The words to watch are house, name and way.

r.h: A house of prayer for all peoples
set: Many scholars think that chapters 56–66 of Isaiah come from the years after the return from Babylon, when the community in Jerusalem was rebuilding its life and asking who truly belonged to God’s people. Chapter 56 opens this last part of the book with a word of welcome.

Two groups felt uncertain. Foreigners had joined themselves to the Lord, perhaps during the exile. Eunuchs had been made so, often in the service of foreign courts. The Law in Deuteronomy 23:1–8 set limits on who could enter the assembly of the Lord. Here, from within Israel’s own Scriptures, the prophet speaks God’s word that those who hold fast to his covenant will not be shut out.
str: v. 1: keep justice, for God’s salvation is near.
v. 2: blessed is the one who keeps the sabbath and does no evil.
v. 3: two fears: the foreigner’s and the eunuch’s.
vv. 4–5: to the faithful eunuchs: a monument and a name.
vv. 6–7: to the faithful foreigners: the holy mountain and the house of prayer for all peoples.
kw: A man who could have no children. In a world where a man lived on in his sons, the eunuch says, “I am just a dry tree.” God answers his deepest fear.
Literally “a hand and a name”, a memorial that keeps someone’s name alive. Israel’s memorial in Jerusalem to the Jewish victims of the Holocaust takes its name, Yad Vashem, from this verse.
The Temple is first of all a place of prayer, and it is meant for “all peoples”. Jesus quotes these words when he cleanses the Temple (Mark 11:17).
vv: Maintain justice, and do what is right, for soon my salvation will come, and my deliverance be revealed.
The order is the same as in the Gospel: God’s salvation is coming, so live rightly now.
do not let the eunuch say, “I am just a dry tree.”
God does not let anyone define himself only by what he lacks.
I will give, in my house and within my walls, a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off.
A promise of a name that lasts, not through children, but through belonging to God’s house.
for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.
This is the high point. The house of Israel’s God is meant to welcome all nations who come to him.
ch: In the Acts of the Apostles, Philip baptizes a eunuch from Ethiopia, a royal official returning from worship in Jerusalem and reading the prophet Isaiah (Acts 8:26–39). The Church sees in him this promise beginning to come true. The Second Vatican Council teaches that all people are called to belong to the new People of God, which is to be spread throughout the whole world (Lumen Gentium 13). The Church does not replace Israel in this; the gifts and the call of God to Israel are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; CCC 839).

set: For the second time the apostles have been arrested for preaching in the name of Jesus. An angel opened the prison, and they were found again teaching in the Temple (5:17–25). Before the council Peter said, “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (5:29). Some of the council were enraged and wanted to kill them (5:33). Then one man stands up.

Gamaliel, called “the Elder”, was one of the most honoured teachers of the Law in his day; Paul later says that he was “brought up … at the feet of Gamaliel” (22:3). Luke presents him with respect, as a wise and fair Jewish teacher. The two examples he gives were real movements. Judas the Galilean led a revolt at the census of AD 6. The Jewish historian Josephus mentions a Theudas who led a movement some years after the time of this speech, so scholars discuss whether Gamaliel had another Theudas in mind or whether Luke has arranged the speech in his own way. The point of the example is clear either way.
str: vv. 34–35: Gamaliel has the apostles put outside and speaks to the council.
vv. 36–37: two leaders whose movements came to nothing.
vv. 38–39: his counsel: if it is of human origin, it will fail; if of God, you cannot stop it.
v. 40: the apostles are flogged and forbidden to speak in the name of Jesus.
vv. 41–42: they leave rejoicing, and every day proclaim Jesus as the Messiah.
kw: A single strong word: “God-fighters”. Gamaliel warns his colleagues that they may find themselves on the wrong side of God.
In the oldest manuscripts Luke says only “the name”, as Jews spoke reverently of “the Name” of God. Now the name of Jesus carries that weight: healing, preaching and suffering are all “for the name”.
A deliberate paradox: they were honoured to be dishonoured. To share Christ’s shame is a privilege.
vv: But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, respected by all the people, stood up
Not every member of the council opposed the apostles. Luke shows a Pharisee speaking for patience and fairness.
because if this plan or this undertaking is of human origin, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them
Good advice, and Luke lets the story prove it true. The Church’s survival through the centuries is itself a kind of answer to Gamaliel’s question, though success alone is never the measure of truth.
As they left the council, they rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name.
Joy after a flogging. The Holy Spirit has changed men who once ran away in fear.
And every day in the temple and at home they did not cease to teach and proclaim Jesus as the Messiah.
Two places for the Gospel: the house of prayer and the family home. The Church grew in both.
ch: The Catechism recalls that from the beginning the core of the Church was often formed by those who had become believers “together with all their household”, and so the Christian family is called the domestic church (CCC 1655–1656; Lumen Gentium 11). St Peter writes in the same spirit as today’s passage: “rejoice insofar as you are sharing Christ’s sufferings” (1 Peter 4:13). The Church does not seek persecution, but she knows that the joy of the risen Lord is stronger than shame.

r.h: Blessed be the God and Father
set: Ephesians opens with a long prayer of blessing. In Greek, vv. 3–14 are a single sentence, one of the longest in the New Testament, as if the writer cannot stop praising. Its form is like the Jewish berakah, the blessing that begins “Blessed are you, Lord our God”.

In some of the oldest manuscripts the words “in Ephesus” are missing from 1:1, and many think the letter was meant to be read in several churches. Many scholars also think it was written by a disciple of Paul in his name; others hold that Paul wrote it. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture.
str: v. 3: blessed be God, who has blessed us in Christ.
vv. 4–6: the Father chose us and destined us to be his children; “to the praise of his glorious grace”.
vv. 7–10: in the Son, redemption through his blood and the mystery of his will: to gather up all things in Christ.
vv. 11–12: our inheritance; “for the praise of his glory”.
vv. 13–14: you were sealed with the Holy Spirit, the pledge of our inheritance; “to the praise of his glory”.
¶ The three refrains mark the work of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
kw: Literally “to sum up under one head”. All things in heaven and earth find their unity and meaning in Christ.
you were marked with the seal
A seal marked ownership and protection. The believer belongs to God and is kept by the Spirit.
A down payment, the first instalment that guarantees the rest. The Spirit we have now is a real share in the glory to come.
vv: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places
God blesses us first; our blessing of God is the answer. All of it is “in Christ”, a phrase that comes again and again in these verses.
In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses
Redemption is the language of setting a slave or captive at liberty at a price. The price is the blood of Christ.
as a plan for the fullness of time, to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
Not only souls are saved; the whole creation is drawn into Christ.
were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit
ch: The Catechism begins its teaching on the Liturgy with this hymn: the whole work of God is a blessing, and the Church answers with blessing (CCC 1077–1078). It also draws on these verses for God’s eternal plan of loving kindness, that we should be his adopted children (CCC 257). St Irenaeus built his teaching on Christ’s “recapitulation” on v. 10: Christ sums up in himself the whole history of humanity, to heal and restore it (Against Heresies, in substance; see CCC 518). The Church links the seal of the Spirit with the anointing of Chrismation, which in the Eastern Churches is given together with Baptism (CCC 1296).

r.h: I am the way, and the truth, and the life
set: It is the night of the Last Supper. Jesus has washed his disciples’ feet, Judas has gone out into the night, and Jesus has told Peter that he will deny him three times (13:36–38). The disciples are afraid. Chapters 14–17 are Jesus’ farewell words to them.

Jesus himself had been “troubled” at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33), at the thought of his hour (12:27) and at the betrayal (13:21). John uses the same verb here. The one who says “Do not let your hearts be troubled” knows what trouble is.
str: vv. 1–4: trust, the Father’s house, a place prepared.
vv. 5–7: Thomas asks about the way; Jesus answers, “I am the way.”
vv. 8–11: Philip asks to see the Father; “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”
vv. 12–14: greater works, and prayer in Jesus’ name.
kw: From the verb menō, to remain or abide, one of John’s favourite words. A monē is a place to stay, not an inn for a night but a home.
Very early, the followers of Jesus were simply called “the Way” (Acts 9:2). Jesus does not only show the way; he is the way.
One of the “I am” sayings of John’s Gospel (bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine). They echo the name God revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14).
vv: Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me.
Jesus asks for the same trust in himself that Israel gives to God. That is already a claim about who he is.
In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.
There is room. No one who comes to the Father through the Son will find the door shut for lack of space.
Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?
Thomas asks the honest question many hearts ask. His question draws out one of the greatest sayings in the Gospel.
I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
The way to the Father is not a method but a person, and he is also the goal: the truth to know and the life to share.
Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
Jesus is the face of the Father. To look at his words and deeds, and above all at his Cross, is to see what God is like.
the one who believes in me will also do the works that I do and, in fact, will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.
The “greater works” are possible only because he goes to the Father and sends the Spirit. They are his works through the Church.
ch: St Augustine says that Christ as God is the homeland to which we go, and Christ as man is the way by which we go (Sermons, in substance). The Catechism teaches that Christ’s whole life is a revelation of the Father, and quotes v. 9 (CCC 516). It also teaches that prayer “in the name of Jesus” is prayer in communion with him, and that the Father gives whatever we ask in that name (CCC 2614). The Second Vatican Council, while it rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, says that the Church proclaims, and must always proclaim, Christ, “the way, the truth, and the life” (Nostra Aetate 2).

qa: Does “No one comes to the Father except through me” mean that people of other religions cannot be saved?

Every salvation comes from Christ through his Church, which is his Body (CCC 846). But those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel or the Church, yet seek God with a sincere heart and, moved by grace, try to do his will as their conscience shows it, can also reach eternal salvation (CCC 847; Lumen Gentium 16). Even then they are saved through Christ, by ways known to God. This is no reason for the Church to stop proclaiming him (CCC 848).
How can believers do “greater works” than Jesus?

Not because they are greater than he is, but because he goes to the Father and works through them by the Spirit. The apostles brought the Gospel to lands Jesus never visited in his earthly life. St Augustine, quoted in the Catechism, says that the justification of a sinner is a greater work than the creation of heaven and earth (CCC 1994).
Why did Gamaliel defend the apostles?

Luke shows him as a wise and devout Pharisee, faithful to the Scriptures, who believed that God would show which movements came from him. He did not become a disciple in Luke’s account, but his fairness protected the apostles that day. His counsel shows that even those outside the Church may serve God’s plan with justice.
rite: In today’s Gospel it is Thomas who asks, “How can we know the way?”, and to him Jesus first says, “I am the way.” The Syro-Malabar Church, whose faith goes back to the preaching of Mar Thoma, has long called its own Christian heritage the Margam, the Way, of Thomas. That way is nothing other than Christ. The Syriac Bible uses raza, mystery, for the “mystery of his will” in Ephesians, and the solemn form of our Holy Qurbana is called the Raza: in the Qurbana the plan of the Father, the redemption by the blood of the Son and the seal of the Spirit are celebrated as one. And as the apostles taught “at home”, our families keep the Gospel alive in the evening family prayer.
study: Isaiah gives the eunuch “a name better than sons and daughters”. Whom does my parish or my family make feel like “a dry tree”, and how could we welcome them?
The apostles rejoiced to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus. What would it cost me this week to speak his name openly, at work or at home?
Ephesians says that I was chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world. How does it change my day to know that I am wanted by God?
Thomas asked, “How can we know the way?” What question would I ask Jesus today, and where do I see him answering it in the Gospel?

lead: The risen Lord will come again, and both readings teach us how to wait. James asks for the patience of a farmer who waits for the rains, and of the prophets and Job, who endured. In the Gospel ten bridesmaids wait for a bridegroom who is delayed; all of them fall asleep, but only five have oil for their lamps when the cry goes up at midnight. Waiting well is not anxious watching of the clock, but steady faithfulness that keeps the lamp supplied. The words to watch are patient, coming and keep awake.

r.h: Be patient until the coming of the Lord
set: The letter of James is a practical letter, full of short teachings like the wisdom books of the Old Testament. Just before today’s verses James has spoken sharply to the rich who withheld the wages of their workers (5:1–6). Now he turns to the poor and the wronged and tells them how to live while they wait for the Lord’s justice.
str: vv. 7–8: be patient like the farmer; the coming of the Lord is near.
v. 9: do not grumble against one another; the Judge is at the doors.
vv. 10–11: examples of endurance: the prophets and Job; the Lord is compassionate.
v. 12: do not swear; let your yes be yes and your no be no.
kw: Literally “be long of spirit”, the opposite of a short temper. The same quality is named among the fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22).
The word for the arrival of a king or an official visit. In the New Testament it is the glorious coming of Christ at the end.
Staying under a load without giving way. It is the endurance of Job, who did not let go of God in his suffering.
vv: Be patient, therefore, beloved, until the coming of the Lord. The farmer waits for the precious crop from the earth, being patient with it until it receives the early and the late rains.

In the land of Israel the early rains came in autumn, at sowing, and the late rains in spring, before harvest (see Deuteronomy 11:14). The farmer cannot make them come; he can only wait and keep working.
Strengthen your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is near.
Patience is not weakness. It needs a strong heart.
Beloved, do not grumble against one another, so that you may not be judged. See, the Judge is standing at the doors!
Hardship tempts a community to turn on itself. James reminds them that the Judge is near, so there is no need to judge one another.
You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
Job’s story ends not with his suffering, but with God’s mercy. That is the “purpose of the Lord”.
ch: The Catechism names patience among the fruits of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1832). On v. 12 it teaches, with the words of Jesus in Matthew 5:33–37 and of St James, that Christians should not swear lightly, and that the Church understands this teaching not to exclude an oath taken for a grave and right reason, as before a court (CCC 2153–2154).

set: This parable comes in Jesus’ last great discourse in Matthew (chapters 24–25), about the end of the age and his coming. It is the first of three parables in chapter 25: the ten bridesmaids, the talents, and the judgment of the nations.

In a village wedding of that time, the bridegroom went to fetch his bride and brought her to his home, often at night, and young women went out with lamps to meet the procession and lead it to the feast. The details of such customs are not fully known, but the picture is clear: a joyful meeting, and a door that is shut at the right time.
str: vv. 1–4: ten bridesmaids, five foolish without oil, five wise with flasks of oil.
v. 5: the bridegroom is delayed; all sleep.
vv. 6–9: the midnight cry; the foolish ask for oil and are refused.
vv. 10–12: the bridegroom comes; the ready go in; the door is shut; “I do not know you.”
v. 13: keep awake.
kw: The wise are the prudent, who think ahead. Mōrai is from the same family as the word Paul uses for the “foolishness” of the Cross (1 Corinthians 1:18). Here foolishness is to live as if the Lord would never come.
A word used of going out to welcome an arriving king or guest and escort him in. Paul uses it for meeting the Lord at his coming (1 Thessalonians 4:17).
The word that ends the parable and runs through Jesus’ teaching on the end. It is not about never sleeping, since all ten slept; it is about being ready.
vv: Ten bridesmaids took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom.
All ten go out. All are invited, all have lamps, all want to meet him. The difference is hidden at first.
As the bridegroom was delayed, all of them became drowsy and slept.
The delay is part of the parable. The early Church learned to live faithfully through a long wait.
No! there will not be enough for you and for us; you had better go to the dealers and buy some for yourselves.
This sounds unkind, but the parable is teaching something else: readiness cannot be borrowed at the last moment. No one can live another person’s faith for them.
Truly I tell you, I do not know you.
Compare Matthew 7:21–23: it is not enough to say “Lord, Lord”. To be known by him is to have lived in friendship with him.
Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
ch: The Second Vatican Council takes up this parable: since we know neither the day nor the hour, we must, as the Lord advised, watch constantly, so that when our earthly life is over we may enter with him into the marriage feast (Lumen Gentium 48, in substance). Many Fathers saw in the oil the good works of love and mercy, which no one can hand over to another at the last moment (in substance). The parable of the judgment that follows (25:31–46) says the same: we are ready for the Lord when we have loved him in the least of his brothers and sisters, and that love is itself his gift in us.

qa: Were the wise bridesmaids selfish when they refused to share their oil?

In real life we are told to share what we have. But a parable makes one point sharply. The oil here stands for something that cannot be lent: a life of faith and love built up over time. At the last moment each person stands before the Lord with his or her own life.
study: James compares patience to a farmer waiting for rain. What am I waiting for from God, and what work can I keep doing while I wait?
What is the “oil” in my lamp, and how will I add to it this week?

lead: Paul ends the oldest of his letters with a string of short commands for a young community: respect those who labour among you, rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks, do not quench the Spirit. In Mark, Jesus explains the parable of the sower: one word falls on four kinds of hearers. Read together, the two readings show what good soil looks like in a parish: people who receive the word with joy, keep it through trouble, and let it bear fruit in prayer, thanksgiving and patience with one another.

set: Thessalonica was the chief city of Macedonia. Paul founded the church there on his second missionary journey and had to leave the city in haste (Acts 17:1–10). He wrote this letter from Corinth, probably about AD 50, and most scholars hold it to be the oldest writing in the New Testament. The community was only a few months old.

Our passage comes at the very end of the letter, just before the closing blessing. After teaching about the Lord's coming (4:13–5:11), Paul gathers his practical counsel into short lines that are easy to remember.
str: vv. 12–13: respect and love for those who lead and labour in the community; peace among all.
vv. 14–15: care for the idle, the fainthearted and the weak; no repaying evil for evil.
vv. 16–18: rejoice, pray, give thanks: three commands and one reason, the will of God in Christ.
vv. 19–22: the Spirit and prophecy: do not quench, do not despise, test, hold fast, abstain.
kw: those who have charge of you

Literally “those who stand before” you. Paul uses the same word for those who lead in Romans 12:8. Within some twenty years of the Resurrection the young Church already had recognised leaders, and Paul asks that they be loved “because of their work”.
Without a break, kept up steadily. Paul uses the same word of his own constant remembering and thanksgiving for this church (1:3; 2:13). He asks of them what he already does for them.
The verb from which the word Eucharist comes. Thanksgiving “in all circumstances” is the habit of a people whose central act of worship is itself a thanksgiving.
vv: Be at peace among yourselves.
Peace in a community is the first fruit of respect for those who serve it.
See that none of you repays evil for evil, but always seek to do good to one another and to all.
“And to all”: kindness does not stop at the church door. Paul echoes the Lord's own teaching (Matthew 5:44; compare Romans 12:17).
Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
People often ask what God's will is for them. Here is one clear answer, and it fits every state of life.
Do not quench the Spirit.
The image is of fire (compare Acts 2:3). The gifts of the Spirit can be put out by neglect or by contempt.
but test everything; hold fast to what is good;
ch: The Second Vatican Council turns to this passage when it speaks of the gifts of the Spirit: those who lead the Church must judge them, not to extinguish the Spirit, but to test all things and hold fast to what is good (Lumen Gentium 12, citing 1 Thessalonians 5:12, 19–21). The Catechism takes “pray constantly” as a description of the Christian life itself (CCC 2742). St Augustine, writing to the widow Proba, explains how this is possible: we pray without ceasing when we go on desiring, in faith, hope and love, the life that God alone can give (in substance).

set: Jesus has told the parable of the sower from a boat to the crowd on the shore (4:1–9). When he is alone with the Twelve and those around him, they ask him about the parables (4:10–12). Now he explains this one, and he treats it as the key to the others: the kingdom comes as a word sown, and everything depends on how it is received.
The explanation moves from the seed to the people. The seed on the path becomes “the ones on the path”. Each kind of ground is a kind of hearer.
str: v. 13: a question to the disciples: if they miss this parable, how will they understand the rest?
v. 14: the sower sows the word.
v. 15: the path: Satan takes the word away at once.
vv. 16–17: rocky ground: joy without root; trouble makes them fall away.
vv. 18–19: thorns: cares, wealth and desires choke the word.
v. 20: good soil: they hear, accept and bear fruit.
kw: In Mark the word is the Gospel message itself (compare 2:2, “he was speaking the word to them”). The first Christians called their preaching simply “the word” (Acts 8:4).
From skandalon, a trap or a stumbling block. Trouble and persecution become a trap that trips them, because there is no root to hold them.
Apatē means deceit. Wealth promises more than it can give, and so it deceives.
vv: The sower sows the word.
Jesus does not stop to describe the sower. In the parable the seed falls everywhere, even where a careful farmer would not throw it. God is generous with his word.
But they have no root, and endure only for a while;
Joy is good, but joy without roots does not last. Roots grow out of sight: in prayer, in the sacraments, in the slow habits of faith.
but the cares of the world, and the lure of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it yields nothing.
Thorns do not kill quickly. They grow up beside the good plant until it has no light.
they hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.
Three verbs: hear, accept, bear fruit. The harvest is far beyond what anyone expected from so much seed that seemed wasted.
ch: St Gregory the Great, preaching on this parable, said that people would hardly believe him if he called riches thorns; yet they are thorns, because they tear the mind with their cares and do not let it rest (in substance). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the word of God is the strength of faith and the food of the soul for the Church's children (Dei Verbum 21). In every Holy Qurbana the word is sown before the Bread of life is given.

qa: Is the parable saying that some people are simply bad soil?

No. The four kinds of ground can be found in one heart, and at different times in one life. The path can be broken up and the thorns pulled out. The parable is a warning and an invitation, not a sentence passed on anyone.
study: Paul asks the community to love those who labour among them. Whom in my parish do I need to thank, or to pray for, this week?
Which of the four kinds of ground best describes my heart this Easter season, and what one thorn do I need to pull out?

lead: Paul writes from prison, weighing life and death, and finds that both belong to Christ: “to me, living is Christ and dying is gain.” In Matthew, a man shut out by his disease kneels before Jesus and says, “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean,” and Jesus touches him. Both readings are about belonging wholly to the Lord: Paul who wants nothing but Christ, and the leper who leaves everything to the Lord's will and is not refused.

set: Paul is in chains (1:7, 13) and does not know whether he will be released or put to death. Where he was imprisoned is debated: Rome, Ephesus and Caesarea have all been proposed. Philippi was the first church he founded in Europe (Acts 16:11–40), and it remained especially dear to him; this is the warmest of his letters.
Just before our passage he has said that Christ will be exalted in his body, “whether by life or by death” (1:20). Now he thinks aloud about which he would choose.
str: v. 21: the principle: life is Christ, death is gain.
vv. 22–24: the dilemma: fruitful labour here, or departing to be with Christ.
vv. 25–26: the decision: for their sake he expects to remain.
kw: A word from business: profit. Two chapters later Paul uses it again: “whatever gains I had, these I have come to regard as loss because of Christ” (3:7).
The verb was used for loosing a ship from its moorings or striking a tent to move on. For Paul, death is a setting out. The POC renders it simply “to die”.
To be held tight from both sides. Paul is not torn between something good and something bad, but between two goods.
vv: For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain.
Not “living is serving Christ”, but “living is Christ”. His whole life has one name.
my desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better;
Paul expects to be with Christ at once after death, not only at the end of time. The Church teaches the same hope (CCC 1011).
but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for you.
Love decides the question. What Paul wants for himself gives way to what the community needs.
I know that I will remain and continue with all of you for your progress and joy in faith,
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on the meaning of Christian death with verse 21: because of Christ, death has a positive meaning (CCC 1010). It adds that the Christian can feel a desire for death like Paul's, “to depart and be with Christ” (CCC 1011). St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom in Rome, wrote in the same spirit that it was better for him to die in Christ Jesus than to reign over the ends of the earth (Letter to the Romans 6, in substance). Paul's choice also teaches that the desire for heaven never excuses us from the work and love owed to others here.

set: Jesus comes down from the mountain after the Sermon (chapters 5–7). Matthew now gathers ten mighty works in chapters 8–9, so that the Lord who has taught with authority is seen to act with authority. The first is the cleansing of a leper.

The law of Leviticus 13–14 kept a person with a skin disease outside the community and gave the priest the task of examining and declaring someone clean. The law protected the people; for the sick person, however, it meant living apart.
str: v. 1: Jesus comes down; the crowds follow.
v. 2: the leper kneels and asks.
v. 3: Jesus stretches out his hand, touches, speaks; the man is clean at once.
v. 4: silence, and the way back through the priest and the offering Moses commanded.
kw: In the Bible the word covers a range of skin diseases, not only what we now call Hansen's disease. What they shared was the separation they brought (Leviticus 13:45–46).
The leper does not doubt the Lord's power; he leaves the matter to his will. Jesus answers with the same word: “I do choose.”
The leper asks to be made clean, not only healed: he asks to be given back to the community and to worship.
vv: and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”
A model of prayer: faith in his power, trust in his will, and no attempt to bargain.
He stretched out his hand and touched him,
The touch comes before the word. Jesus could have healed from a distance; he chose to touch a man no one would touch.
“I do choose. Be made clean!” Immediately his leprosy was cleansed.
go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.
Jesus respects the law of Moses and sends the man back into the life of his people.
ch: Many Fathers, among them St John Chrysostom, notice that when the Lord touched the leper his hand did not become unclean; instead the leper became clean (in substance). The Catechism sees in Christ's compassion for the sick, and in his many healings, the sign that God has visited his people (CCC 1503). The leper's words, “Lord, if you choose”, have become a prayer of the Church for every sickness of body and soul.

qa: Why does Jesus tell the man to say nothing to anyone?

Matthew, following Mark, often shows Jesus avoiding public fame from his miracles. He did not want to be followed only as a wonder worker, and his mission would be fully understood only after the Cross and the Resurrection. Here the man is also sent first to the priest, so that his healing becomes a witness through the proper path of the law.
study: Paul can say “living is Christ”. What one word would honestly describe what my life is about at present?
The leper prayed, “Lord, if you choose.” Can I bring my most pressing need to the Lord this week in those words?

lead: Paul holds up the poor churches of Macedonia, who in their poverty begged to give, and he grounds their generosity in Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor”. In Mark, the disciples cry out in a storm while Jesus sleeps in the stern, and he stills the wind and the sea with a word. Both readings ask where our security lies: not in what we hold, nor in calm water, but in the Lord who gave himself and who is in the boat with us.

set: For several years Paul organised a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; Galatians 2:10). For him it was more than relief: it was a sign that Jews and Gentiles who believed in Christ were one Church.

The Corinthians had begun the collection a year earlier and then let it slip. Paul does not command; he tells them what the churches of Macedonia, Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea among them, have done, and points them to Christ.
str: vv. 1–5: the example of Macedonia: affliction, poverty, joy, and generosity beyond their means.
v. 6: Titus is sent to complete the work in Corinth.
vv. 7–8: excel in this as in everything; not a command, but a test of love.
v. 9: the reason: the self-giving of Christ.
vv. 10–11: finish what you began, according to your means.
kw: The key word of the chapter. The NRSV gives it as “grace” (v. 1), “privilege” (v. 4), “generous undertaking” (vv. 6–7) and “generous act” (v. 9). Paul calls the collection itself a grace: giving is first something God gives.
Fellowship, communion, partnership. The Macedonians beg for a share in the service of the saints. The same word describes the life of the first community in Acts 2:42.
The verb means to become a beggar, to be reduced to poverty. Paul is speaking of the whole self-emptying of the Son, from the Incarnation to the Cross (compare Philippians 2:6–8).
vv: their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
Joy and poverty together produce generosity. Generosity does not depend on having much.
they gave themselves first to the Lord and, by the will of God, to us,
The order matters. A gift of money that does not come from a gift of self is not yet what Paul is asking for.
though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.
The whole Gospel in one sentence. Christian giving is a share in this exchange.
now finish doing it, so that your eagerness may be matched by completing it according to your means.
Good intentions are not enough. Paul asks for what is possible, “according to your means”, but asks that it be done.
ch: The Catechism links the collection made at the Holy Qurbana with this very verse: from the beginning Christians brought, with the bread and wine, gifts to share with those in need, following the example of Christ who became poor to make us rich (CCC 1351). It cites St Justin's description of the Sunday gathering in the second century, where those who have means give what they wish, and the one who presides helps orphans, widows and all in need (First Apology 67).

r.h: Even the wind and the sea obey him
set: The same day Jesus taught in parables from the boat (4:1), he tells his disciples to cross the Sea of Galilee to the other side, the region of the Gerasenes (5:1), largely Gentile country. The lake lies far below sea level among hills, and sudden violent winds are well known there.

For Israel the sea was a picture of chaos, which only God can master (Psalm 89:9; Psalm 107:23–30). Jonah too slept in a ship in a storm (Jonah 1:5). Mark's account invites the question with which it ends: who then is this?
str: vv. 35–36: evening; they set out, taking him “just as he was”.
v. 37: the storm.
v. 38: Jesus asleep; the disciples' cry.
v. 39: the rebuke and the calm.
vv. 40–41: Jesus' question about faith; their question about him.
kw: The same verb Mark used when Jesus rebuked an unclean spirit in the synagogue at Capernaum (1:25). Jesus speaks to the storm as to a hostile power.
Literally “be muzzled”. It is the same verb as “Be silent!” spoken to the unclean spirit (1:25).
they were filled with great awe
Literally “they feared a great fear”. Their fear of the storm becomes the awe of people who stand before God at work.
vv: But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion;
Only Mark mentions the cushion. The detail sounds like an eyewitness memory. His sleep is the sleep of trust (Psalm 4:8).
Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?
It is the cry of many believers in many storms. The Lord does not rebuke them for crying out, only for being afraid.
“Peace! Be still!” Then the wind ceased, and there was a dead calm.
Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?
Faith here is not the absence of storms, but trust in the One who is in the boat.
Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
The disciples answer without knowing it: only the Lord commands the sea (Psalm 107:29).
ch: Tertullian saw the little boat as a figure of the Church, tossed by the waves of the world while the Lord seems to sleep (On Baptism 12, in substance). St Augustine applied the scene to each heart: when we are insulted and the waves rise, it is because Christ is asleep in us, that is, our faith has fallen asleep; wake him, and the storm is calmed (in substance). Pope Francis meditated on this passage during the pandemic, on 27 March 2020, in an empty St Peter's Square, reminding the world that we are all in the same boat.

study: The Macedonians “gave themselves first to the Lord”. What would it look like for my family to give ourselves first, and then our gifts?
What storm am I in at present, and how can I let the Lord's question, “Why are you afraid?”, become an invitation to trust?

lead: Paul asks the strong in Rome to bear with the weak and not to please themselves, “for Christ did not please himself.” In Luke, on a sabbath, Jesus places a man with a withered hand in the middle of the synagogue and asks whether it is lawful to do good or to do harm. Both readings measure religion by the good done to the neighbour: the strong carry the weak, and the day of the Lord becomes a day of healing.

set: In Romans 14 Paul has addressed a dispute in the Roman community over food and the keeping of days. Some, whom he calls “weak” in faith, kept scruples about these things; others, the “strong”, felt no such need. Paul counts himself among the strong (15:1), but his whole concern is that no one should be pushed into acting against conscience, and that the community stay one.
This passage draws the argument together and grounds it in Christ.
str: vv. 1–2: the duty of the strong: bear with the weak, build up the neighbour.
v. 3: the reason: Christ, in the words of Psalm 69.
v. 4: why the Scriptures were written: steadfastness, encouragement, hope.
vv. 5–6: a prayer for harmony, ending in one voice of praise.
kw: Not flattery, but seeking someone's good. Paul says elsewhere that he tries to please everyone “so that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians 10:33).
A word from building a house. The test of my freedom is whether it builds up my neighbour or knocks something down in him.
With one mind. The same word describes the first community praying together in Acts 1:14 and gathering in the Temple in Acts 2:46.
vv: We who are strong ought to put up with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
Strength in faith is given for carrying others, not for looking down on them.
The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.
Psalm 69:9. The first Christians read this psalm as the prayer of Christ in his Passion (compare John 2:17; 19:28–29).
For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, so that by steadfastness and by the encouragement of the scriptures we might have hope.
A charter for reading the Old Testament: it is written for us, and its purpose is hope.
so that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Harmony is not an end in itself. It is for worship: a divided community cannot sing with one voice.
ch: The Catechism draws from Romans 14 one of its rules for conscience: charity always respects the neighbour and his conscience, so that we do nothing that makes a brother stumble (CCC 1789). Paul asks the strong to carry the weak, as Christ carried our burdens (compare Galatians 6:2). The Holy Qurbana is where the Church learns to glorify God “with one voice”.

r.h: To do good on the sabbath
set: This is the second of two sabbath disputes in Luke 6 (vv. 1–5: the disciples pick grain). The sabbath was God's gift to Israel, a day of rest and of holiness, and keeping it faithfully was a mark of loyalty to the covenant. Jewish teachers agreed that saving a life set aside the sabbath rest; the question here is a man whose life is not in danger. Could the healing not wait until the next day?
Luke alone notes that it was the man's right hand, the hand he would need for work.
str: v. 6: Jesus teaching in the synagogue; the man with the withered hand.
v. 7: scribes and Pharisees watching.
v. 8: Jesus calls the man into the middle.
v. 9: the question: good or harm, to save life or to destroy it.
v. 10: the look, the word, the healing.
v. 11: their anger.
kw: The question of what the law allows. Jesus turns it from “what may be done” to “what good may be done”.
Life, the whole living person. To fail to do good when one can is, in Jesus' question, a kind of harm.
Literally “mindlessness”, a rage that no longer reasons. Luke's ending is quieter than Mark's (Mark 3:6): they only discuss what they might do.
vv: and there was a man there whose right hand was withered.
Come and stand here.
The Greek says “stand in the middle”, as the POC has it. Jesus does not heal in a corner. The man who has been at the edge is placed at the centre.
I ask you, is it lawful to do good or to do harm on the sabbath, to save life or to destroy it?
There is no neutral ground: the day of God is a day for doing good.
“Stretch out your hand.” He did so, and his hand was restored.
Jesus does no work that anyone could call labour; he speaks, and the man obeys. The healing comes in the obeying.
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of the sabbath, and gives this law its authentic and authoritative interpretation: the sabbath is for doing good rather than harm, for saving life rather than killing (CCC 2173, citing Mark 3:4). For Christians the Lord's Day, Sunday, keeps this spirit: it is a day for the Holy Qurbana, and also for works of mercy and time given to the sick, the old and the lonely (CCC 2186).

study: Who in my family or parish is “weak” in some way that I find irritating? How can I carry that person this week instead of judging?
Jesus called the man into the middle. Who is at the edge of our community, and how can we bring that person to the centre?

lead: James asks what good it is to say “I have faith” and to send away a hungry brother or sister with kind words: faith without works is dead. In Luke, Jesus ends his sermon by asking why we call him “Lord, Lord” and do not do what he says, and he compares the one who hears and acts to a man who dug deep and built on rock. Both readings call for a faith that reaches the hands. Such works are not our own achievement; they are the fruit of grace in those who believe.

set: The Letter of James is a practical letter, close in spirit to the Sermon on the Mount. It has already warned against favouring the rich in the assembly (2:1–7). Now it turns to a faith that speaks but does nothing.

James and Paul use the same words in different ways. Paul denies that we are justified by “works of the law” (Romans 3:28), meaning the law of Moses as a way to earn standing before God. James is speaking of the works of love that living faith produces. The Church holds both together.
str: v. 14: two questions: what good is it? can that faith save?
vv. 15–16: an example: the hungry brother or sister and the empty blessing.
v. 17: the conclusion: faith by itself, without works, is dead.
kw: In v. 14 the Greek has the article, “the faith” or “that faith”: the faith just described, which has no works. The POC brings this out: “this faith” (ഈ വിശ്വാസത്തിന്). James is not doubting the power of true faith.
Not rituals, but deeds of mercy: clothing the naked, feeding the hungry (compare Matthew 25:35–36).
Like a body without breath (2:26). Such faith may look whole, but it has no life in it.
vv: What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if you say you have faith but do not have works? Can faith save you?
The stress falls on “say”. James is speaking of a faith that is only talk.
Go in peace; keep warm and eat your fill,
A blessing that costs nothing and gives nothing. The words are pious; the hunger remains.
So faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead.
ch: The Catechism teaches that faith without works is dead: when it is deprived of hope and love, faith does not fully unite the believer to Christ and does not make him a living member of his Body (CCC 1815, citing James 2:26). The Council of Trent taught that we are justified by grace, which we cannot earn, and that the justified, by keeping God's commandments and doing good works, grow in that justice by the same grace (Session 6). St Augustine put it simply: good works follow justification; they do not come before it (On Faith and Works, in substance).

set: These verses close the Sermon on the Plain (6:20–49), Luke's shorter counterpart of Matthew's Sermon on the Mount. The sermon has taught love of enemies, mercy, not judging, and good fruit from a good heart. Now Jesus asks what we will do with it.
Luke's picture differs a little from Matthew's (7:24–27): one man digs deep to rock, and the danger is a river in flood bursting against the house.
str: v. 46: the question: why call me “Lord” and not do what I say?
v. 47: the one who comes, hears and acts.
v. 48: the house dug deep, set on rock, unshaken by the flood.
v. 49: the house without a foundation, and its great ruin.
kw: The title Christians gave the risen Jesus, and the cry of the Church's prayer. The words are right; Jesus asks that the life match them.
Literally “he went deep”. Building on rock costs digging. The foundation is hidden, but everything depends on it.
Paul uses the same word: “no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid; that foundation is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).
vv: Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I tell you?
That one is like a man building a house, who dug deeply and laid the foundation on rock;
Two men may build houses that look alike. The difference is below the ground, and it shows only in the flood.
the river burst against that house but could not shake it, because it had been well built.
The flood comes to both houses. Faith does not spare us the flood; it keeps us standing in it.
When the river burst against it, immediately it fell, and great was the ruin of that house.
The sermon ends on a warning, not on a threat: Jesus is telling us the truth while there is time to dig.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of prayer, recalls that the prayer of faith does not consist only in saying “Lord, Lord”, but in disposing the heart to do the will of the Father (CCC 2611). Pope Benedict XVI wrote that those who build their lives on the word of God build on rock that does not give way (Verbum Domini, in substance). Every Holy Qurbana sends us out to do what we have heard.

qa: Do James and Paul contradict each other?

No. Paul teaches that we cannot earn God's favour; justification is the gift of grace received in faith (Ephesians 2:8–9). James teaches that true faith is alive and acts in love. Paul himself speaks of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). The works of the justified are themselves God's gift and also truly ours, and by grace they please God.
study: James describes a blessing that costs nothing. Whose need have I answered only with words, and what one practical thing can I do this week?
Where in my life am I building without digging deep, and what would it mean to put my foundation on the Lord's words?

lead: On this fourth Sunday of the Resurrection, kept as the World Prayer Day for Vocations, the readings move from sorrow to joy. Isaiah hears Zion say, “The Lord has forsaken me,” and God answers that a mother may forget her nursing child, “yet I will not forget you.” In Acts, the Holy Spirit is given in Samaria through the laying on of the apostles' hands, and Simon learns that God's gift cannot be bought. Ephesians tells those who were dead in sin that God, rich in mercy, has made them alive and seated them with Christ. In John, Jesus promises that the disciples' pain will turn into joy, like the joy of a mother when her child is born.

The thread is a gift no one can earn or seize: God's faithful love, the Spirit, salvation by grace, a joy no one can take away. Vocations belong to the same order: a call is received, never bought. The calendar notes the fuller passages Ephesians 1:15–2:7 and John 16:16–33; the exegesis follows the readings as listed.

set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC, after Jerusalem and its Temple had been destroyed. Many scholars attribute these chapters to a prophet of the exile writing in the tradition of Isaiah. They open with the words “Comfort, O comfort my people” (40:1).

In our passage the city of Zion, Jerusalem, is pictured as a woman: a wife who thinks herself abandoned and a mother who has lost her children. God answers her complaint, and the answer grows into a vision of the city crowded with returning children, carried by the nations.
str: v. 13: a call to heaven and earth to rejoice: the Lord has comforted his people.
v. 14: Zion's complaint: forsaken, forgotten.
vv. 15–16: God's answer: more faithful than a mother; Zion inscribed on his palms.
vv. 17–21: the ruins filled with children; the bereaved mother astonished.
vv. 22–23: the nations carry Zion's sons and daughters home; those who wait for the Lord shall not be put to shame.
kw: The Hebrew word for compassion is related to reḥem, womb. In v. 15 the two meet: “show no compassion for the child of her womb”. God's mercy is described with the most tender bond we know.
To cut into a surface so that it cannot be erased. God has not merely written Zion's name down; he has engraved it on his own hands.

A guardian who carries a child (compare Numbers 11:12, where Moses complains that he must carry the people “as a nurse carries a sucking child”). In v. 23 kings become foster fathers to Zion's children.
vv: For the Lord has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his suffering ones.
The song of joy comes before the complaint. God's comfort is announced first, as Easter is announced to disciples still in grief.
The Lord has forsaken me, my Lord has forgotten me.
Scripture lets Zion say this aloud. Complaint, too, can be prayer, as in the Psalms.
Can a woman forget her nursing child, or show no compassion for the child of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.
God does not deny that human love can fail. He says that his own love does not.
See, I have inscribed you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me.
Christians can hardly hear this verse without thinking of the risen Lord, who showed his disciples his hands (John 20:20, 27).
Who has borne me these?
The barren mother finds herself surrounded by children she did not expect. It is a picture of the Church gathered from the nations.
those who wait for me shall not be put to shame.
The image before it, of kings bowing and licking the dust, is the court language of the ancient world for complete submission. The promise at the end is the point: waiting on God is never wasted.
ch: The Catechism quotes verses 14–15 to show that God's love for his people is stronger than a mother's love for her children (CCC 219), and it teaches that God's parental tenderness can be expressed by the image of motherhood, though God is neither man nor woman (CCC 239; 370). Pope John Paul I said in a brief Angelus of 1978 that God is our Father, and even more our Mother (in substance). The Church has also seen in the crowded city of vv. 18–23 a picture of herself, the Mother of many children, gathered from all peoples.

set: After the death of Stephen, a persecution scattered the believers from Jerusalem (8:1). Philip, one of the Seven chosen in Acts 6:5, went down to Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah there. Many believed and were baptised, among them Simon, a man who had amazed the city with magic (8:9–13).

Samaritans and Jews were long divided over the place of worship and the Scriptures (compare John 4:9, 20). That the word of God was received in Samaria was a great step outward, as the risen Lord had foretold: “in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8).
str: vv. 14–17: the apostles send Peter and John; prayer and the laying on of hands; the Spirit is received.
vv. 18–19: Simon offers money for the power to give the Spirit.
vv. 20–23: Peter's rebuke and call to repentance.
v. 24: Simon asks for prayer.
v. 25: the apostles preach in many Samaritan villages on the way home.
kw: The laying on of hands is a gesture of blessing and of handing on in Scripture. Here it is joined to prayer for the gift of the Spirit.
A gift given without payment. Luke uses it of the Holy Spirit in Peter's Pentecost sermon (2:38). By its nature a gift cannot be bought.
The phrase recalls Deuteronomy 29:18, a root that bears “poisonous and bitter growth”: a heart turned away from God. The POC renders the sense as deep resentment.
vv: prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit
The apostles begin with prayer. The Spirit is asked for, not produced.
Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
John, who once wanted fire from heaven on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54), now brings the Holy Spirit to Samaritans.
May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain God’s gift with money!
From Simon's name comes the word simony: buying or selling spiritual things.
your heart is not right before God.
Peter goes to the root. The money is a symptom; the heart that wants to possess holy power is the illness.
Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may happen to me.
Luke leaves the story open. Simon at least asks for the apostles' prayer.
ch: The Catechism reads this passage as a witness to the sacrament later called Confirmation: from the time of the apostles, the gift of the Spirit that completes the grace of Baptism was given by the laying on of hands (CCC 1288; 1315). It names Simon's sin: simony is the buying or selling of spiritual things (CCC 2121). St Irenaeus counted Simon as the father of heresies (Against Heresies 1.23), and St Cyril of Jerusalem warned those preparing for Baptism that Simon came to the water and was baptised but was not enlightened, because his heart was not open (Procatechesis 2, in substance).

set: Ephesians is one of the letters whose authorship is discussed: tradition and many scholars hold it to be Paul's, written from prison, while others think it was written by a disciple in his name. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.

In chapter 1 the letter has blessed God for choosing, adopting and redeeming us, and has prayed that we may know the power that raised Christ from the dead (1:19–20). Now it shows that the same power has worked in us: the God who raised Christ has raised us, who were dead.
str: vv. 1–3: what we were: dead in trespasses, following the world and the evil one, children of wrath.
v. 4: the turn: “But God”.
vv. 5–6: what God has done: made alive, raised up, seated with Christ.
v. 7: why: to show the riches of his grace in the ages to come.
kw: God's wealth is mercy. Pope John Paul II took the title of his encyclical on the mercy of God, Dives in Misericordia (1980), from this verse.
Three verbs in vv. 5–6 begin with the Greek prefix for “with”: made alive with, raised with, seated with. What happened to Christ at Easter has happened to us with him.
by grace you have been saved
The verb is in the perfect tense: a past act whose effect lasts. Salvation is God's gift; the letter repeats it in v. 8.
vv: You were dead through the trespasses and sins
Not merely weak or sick, but dead. The dead cannot raise themselves.
But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us
Two words that turn the whole story. Everything after them is God's work.
made us alive together with Christ
and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,
The verbs are past. In Baptism our life is already joined to the risen Lord, though we still await its full revealing (Colossians 3:3–4).
the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
ch: The Council of Trent drew on verse 3, “by nature children of wrath”, in its teaching on the state of humanity after Adam's sin (Session 6, chapter 1). The Catechism teaches that our justification comes from the grace of God, the undeserved help he gives us to respond to his call (CCC 1996). Easter is the feast of this passage: the Church baptises in the season of the Resurrection because Baptism is our rising with Christ (Romans 6:4).

r.h: Your pain will turn into joy
set: These words belong to the Last Discourse, spoken by Jesus at the supper on the night before he died (John 13–17). He has told his disciples that he is going to the Father and that the Advocate will come (16:5–15). Now he speaks of a short absence and a return.

The Church reads these words in the season of the Resurrection because they were fulfilled at Easter: the disciples did not see him while he lay in the tomb, and then they saw him again, and their grief became joy (20:20).
str: v. 16: the riddle: “a little while”.
vv. 17–19: the disciples' puzzled questions, and Jesus' awareness of them.
v. 20: weeping and joy.
v. 21: the image of a woman in labour.
v. 22: “I will see you again”: a joy no one can take.
vv. 23–24: asking the Father in Jesus' name.
kw: The phrase occurs seven times in vv. 16–19. The disciples cannot understand it; the reader knows it means the three days between death and Resurrection, and also the whole time until the Lord comes again.
Grief and pain of body and heart. The same word is used of the woman in labour (v. 21): the sorrow is real, but it is the sorrow of a birth.

Verse 23 uses two different verbs: “you will ask (erōtaō, question) nothing of me”, but “if you ask (aiteō, request) anything of the Father”. On that day the disciples will no longer need to question him; they will be able to ask the Father directly in his name.
vv: A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.
you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
Not replaced by joy, but turned into it. The same Cross that caused the grief becomes the source of the joy.
When a woman is in labor, she has pain, because her hour has come.

“Hour” is the word John uses for the Lord's Passion (12:23; 13:1). The prophets compared the birth of God's new people to a woman in labour (Isaiah 26:17; 66:7–9). Many interpreters also think here of the Mother of Jesus, whom he calls “Woman” at the Cross (19:26), and of the new family born there.
but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.
Earlier he said “you will see me”; now, “I will see you”. The joy rests not on our sight of him, but on his faithful gaze upon us.
Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.
Prayer in his name is the place where Easter joy grows.
ch: St Augustine read the “little while” as the whole of this present age, short when seen from its end: now we grieve because we long for the Lord and do not yet see him, but soon we shall see him, and there no one will take our joy away (Tractates on John 101, in substance). The Catechism teaches that there is no other way of Christian prayer than Christ, and that our prayer has access to the Father only if we pray in the name of Jesus (CCC 2664).

qa: Why had the Samaritans not received the Holy Spirit when they were baptised?

Luke does not explain it fully. He shows that the new community in Samaria was joined to the apostles of Jerusalem, so that the Church remained one, and that the gift of the Spirit came through their prayer and the laying on of their hands. The Catechism sees here the origin of the sacrament that completes Baptism (CCC 1288; 1315). In the Eastern Churches, including the Syro-Malabar Church, this anointing is given together with Baptism, and the oil used is consecrated by the Major Archbishop, which keeps the link with the apostles (CCC 1290–1292).
Does God really compare himself to a mother?

Yes. Isaiah does so here and again in 66:13. God is neither man nor woman; he is pure spirit, and the perfections of both father and mother are found in him (CCC 239; 370). Scripture and the Church call God Father, as Jesus taught us, and the image of a mother shows the tenderness of that same love.
If we ask anything in Jesus' name, why are some prayers not answered as we hope?

To ask in his name is to ask as he would ask, in union with his will. The Catechism speaks honestly of the trial of prayer that seems not to be heard, and reminds us with James that we may ask wrongly (CCC 2735–2737). The Father always gives what is truly good, and above all the Holy Spirit (Luke 11:13).
rite: The Syro-Malabar Church keeps this Sunday, like the universal Church, as the World Prayer Day for Vocations. Our families have given many priests and religious to the Church in India and far beyond. Isaiah's barren mother, astonished at her children, and Simon's attempt to buy what can only be received, together teach the right spirit: a vocation is a gift received in prayer, and for priests through the laying on of hands; it is never a career to be acquired.

In our tradition the newly baptised child is anointed with the holy oil (Mooron) at the same celebration, so that the gift of the Spirit that Peter and John brought to Samaria is given at the very start of Christian life. The Queen of Heaven is prayed until Pentecost; with it we greet Mary, the Mother whose sorrow at the Cross was turned into the joy of the Resurrection.
study: Zion said, “The Lord has forgotten me.” When have I felt forgotten by God, and what does it mean to me that my name is written on his hands?
Simon wanted to own the power of the Spirit. In what ways can I treat holy things, roles in the parish or the Church itself as something I possess?
Ephesians says that I have been raised and seated with Christ. How would my week be different if I believed this was already true of me?
What sorrow in my family could the Lord turn into joy? Whom in my family or parish will I pray for this week, that they may hear and answer God's call?

lead: Both readings today put a son in front of hostile power. Paul charges Timothy “in the presence of God” and of Christ Jesus, who “made the good confession” before Pontius Pilate, and he ends with a hymn to the God who dwells in unapproachable light. In Luke, the owner of a vineyard sends servant after servant to his tenants, and last of all his beloved son, whom they throw out and kill. In this season the Church hears the parable knowing how the story ended: the Son who was rejected is risen. The key words are confession, appearing and heir.

set: The First Letter to Timothy closes with a solemn charge to a young leader of the church at Ephesus. The letter presents itself as Paul's; many scholars think it was written later in Paul's name by a disciple, while others hold that it is his own. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.

Just before these verses Paul reminds Timothy of the confession he made “in the presence of many witnesses” (6:12), most likely at his baptism or his ordination. Now he sets that confession beside the confession of Christ himself.
str: v. 13: the charge, given before God the giver of life and before Christ the faithful witness.
v. 14: keep the commandment until the Lord appears.
vv. 15–16: a hymn to God, the only Sovereign, who alone has immortality.
kw: To say the same thing, to agree openly. It is used of Timothy's confession in v. 12 and of Christ's in v. 13. The Christian's word of faith echoes the word Christ spoke at his trial.
A shining forth. The Pastoral Letters prefer this word for the Lord's return, and they also use it for his first coming (2 Timothy 1:10).
Found only here in the New Testament. God is not far away by choice; his light is simply beyond what creatures can reach, unless he comes near to us.
vv: In the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, I charge you
This is the only place in the letters of Paul where Pilate is named. The Creed keeps the same memory: “suffered under Pontius Pilate”. Our faith is tied to a real trial, on a real day.
It is he alone who has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see; to him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
Many scholars think Paul is quoting a hymn the church already sang. The God no one can see has been made known in the Son (John 1:18).
ch: The Catechism recalls that before Pilate Christ declared that he came into the world “to bear witness to the truth”, and that the Christian is called not to be ashamed of testifying to the Lord (CCC 2471). Every confession of faith made at baptism, in the Creed of the Holy Qurbana, or before a hostile world shares in that first confession. The doxology of v. 16 has passed into Christian prayer: we adore a God who is beyond us, and we approach him only because he has approached us.

r.h: I will send my beloved son
set: Jesus is teaching in the Temple in the last days before his Passion. The chief priests, the scribes and the elders have just asked him by what authority he acts (20:1–8). He answers with a parable told to the people, but aimed, as Luke says, at those leaders (20:19).

Every listener would have heard Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), where the vineyard is the house of Israel. Absentee landlords and quarrels with tenants were also a familiar part of life in Galilee.
str: v. 9: the vineyard planted and leased.
vv. 10–12: three servants, each treated worse.
v. 13: the owner's decision: “my beloved son”.
vv. 14–15a: the plot and the killing outside the vineyard.
vv. 15b–16: the owner's response, and the people's cry, “Heaven forbid!”
kw: The words of the Father's voice at the Jordan (Luke 3:22). The parable has its hearers understand who the last messenger is.
Only Luke has the owner say “perhaps they will respect him”. It is the hope of a father who keeps trying, even when the servants have been beaten.
The tenants think that by killing the heir they will gain the inheritance. In the Easter faith the opposite happens: the heir is raised and shares the inheritance with all who are his (Romans 8:17).
vv: I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.
The question “What shall I do?” is the question of a God who will not give up on his vineyard.
So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.
Luke and Matthew put the throwing out before the killing. Hebrews remembers that Jesus suffered outside the city gate (Hebrews 13:12).
He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.
The vineyard is not destroyed; the unfaithful tenants are. The warning is to those entrusted with the care of God's people in every age, the shepherds of the Church included.
ch: The Fathers, St Irenaeus among them, read the servants as the prophets and the son as Christ (in substance). The Church reads the parable as a word about her Lord's Passion, and never as a charge against the Jewish people: Luke shows that the people hung on his words, and that the leaders of that day were the ones addressed (19:48; 20:19; CCC 597). In the Resurrection the rejected Son becomes, in the verse that follows the reading, the cornerstone (20:17; Psalm 118:22).

qa: Does “give the vineyard to others” mean that God has rejected Israel?

No. In Luke the parable is addressed to the leaders who rejected Jesus, and the people themselves cry out against the thought of such an ending. Paul teaches that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29), and the Church holds that the Jewish people remain beloved of God (CCC 839). The new tenants are the apostles and their successors, who will be judged by the same standard.
study: Where am I asked today to make “the good confession”, at work, at home or among friends?
The owner keeps sending, even after the servants are beaten. Where has God kept sending to me when I did not respond?

lead: Both readings are about wealth and what it can and cannot buy. Paul tells Timothy what to say to the rich: do not be haughty, do not hope in riches, be rich in good works, and so “take hold of the life that really is life”. In Matthew, after the rich young man has gone away sad, Jesus says that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom, and then adds that for God all things are possible. The key words are hope, deposit and hundredfold.

r.h: The life that really is life
set: After the solemn doxology of vv. 15–16 the letter returns to practical matters. Ephesus was a rich commercial city, and the church there included people of means. Earlier in the chapter the letter warned those who want to be rich (6:9–10); now it speaks to those who already are.
The last verses go back to the letter's first concern: false teaching (1:3–7). Timothy is to guard what he has received and avoid empty talk.
str: vv. 17–19: a charge to the rich: hope in God, do good, share, and so lay up a good foundation.
vv. 20–21a: guard the deposit; avoid what is falsely called knowledge.
v. 21b: the blessing.
kw: the life that really is life
Riches give a life that looks like life. The letter points to the life that is real, the life of God which begins now and lasts.
From the same root as koinōnia, communion. Sharing goods is the outward side of sharing in the one life of Christ.
what has been entrusted, the deposit
A legal word for something left in another's safekeeping, to be returned intact. The Catechism uses this text for the deposit of faith entrusted by the apostles to the whole Church (CCC 84).
vv: As for those who in the present age are rich, command them not to be haughty, or to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but rather on God who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment.
The letter does not condemn the good things of creation; God gives them “for our enjoyment”. The danger lies in pride and in false hope.
so that they may take hold of the life that really is life.
Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you.

The phrase “what is falsely called knowledge” (in Greek, pseudōnymos gnōsis) gave St Irenaeus the title of his great work against the Gnostics, the “Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called”.
ch: The Church teaches the universal destination of goods: what we own is given to us also for others (CCC 2402–2406). Generosity is one way of laying up treasure in heaven, as the Lord said (Matthew 6:20), and it is done by grace, not to buy grace. The command to guard the deposit stands behind the Church's care to hand on the faith whole, the faith which the apostles received from the Lord and which the Holy Spirit keeps alive in her (CCC 84).

r.h: For God all things are possible
set: A rich young man has just asked Jesus what good deed he must do to have eternal life. Told to sell his possessions and follow, he went away grieving, “for he had many possessions” (19:22). Jesus now turns to his disciples.
In the thinking of the time, riches were often taken as a sign of God's blessing (compare Deuteronomy 28:1–14). That is why the disciples are so astounded: if the blessed cannot be saved, who can?
str: vv. 23–24: the hardness of entering the kingdom for the rich; the camel and the needle.
vv. 25–26: “Who can be saved?” “For God all things are possible.”
v. 27: Peter's question: what will we have?
vv. 28–29: the reward of the Twelve and of all who leave everything.
v. 30: the first and the last.
kw: The largest animal in Palestine and the smallest opening anyone knew: a deliberate picture of the impossible. The popular story of a small city gate called “the needle's eye” has no ancient evidence behind it. A few late manuscripts read kamilos, “rope”, which shows that some readers found the saying too hard.
Literally “new birth”. It is used here of the renewal of the world at the end, and in Titus 3:5 of baptism. Both meanings belong together: the new creation begins in the font.
An overflowing return. Mark adds that it comes “with persecutions” (Mark 10:30).
