vv: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.
For mortals it is impossible, but for God all things are possible.
Jesus does not soften his saying; he points beyond human strength. The same truth was spoken to Abraham (Genesis 18:14) and to the Virgin Mary at the Annunciation (Luke 1:37).
everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or fields, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold, and will inherit eternal life.
“For my name's sake” is the key. Loss for its own sake is not the point; love of the Lord is.
ch: Clement of Alexandria, in his little book Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, taught that the Lord asks us to banish from the soul the passion for wealth more than wealth itself, and to use what we have for others (in substance). The Catechism speaks of poverty of heart: Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544–2547). Every vocation that leaves home and fields for the Lord, the priest's, the religious sister's or brother's and the missionary's, lives from this promise.

qa: Is it wrong to be rich?

No. Abraham and Job were rich, and the letter to Timothy speaks of God who gives us everything “for our enjoyment”. The danger is to trust in riches, to be proud because of them, and to keep them from those in need. What is impossible for us, a heart loosened from that grip, God can give.
study: Where do I set my hope: on what I have, or on God who gives it?
What has the Lord asked me to leave for his name's sake, and what “hundredfold” have I already received?

lead: Today's readings are joined by the word witness. Hebrews looks at Melchizedek, the priest-king who blessed Abraham, and draws its conclusion from a short phrase: he is one “of whom it is testified that he lives”. In John, Jesus names the witnesses that stand behind him: John the Baptist, the works the Father gave him to do, and the Father himself. In the Easter season both point to the same truth: the priest who lives for ever is the risen Son. The key words are priest, testimony and works.

r.h: A priest according to the order of Melchizedek
set: Hebrews is a long sermon in written form, whose author is not named. Its great theme is that Christ is our high priest. Jesus did not belong to the priestly tribe of Levi, so the author turns to Psalm 110:4, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”, and to the only story about Melchizedek, in Genesis 14:18–20.

In Genesis, Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, meets Abraham after a battle, brings out bread and wine, and blesses him; Abraham gives him a tenth of everything. Hebrews reads the passage closely, paying attention even to what it does not say.
str: vv. 1–3: who Melchizedek is: his names, and the silence about his origin and end.
vv. 4–7: his greatness: he received a tenth from Abraham and blessed him.
vv. 8–10: he “lives”; even Levi paid tithes through Abraham.
kw: In Hebrew the name means “my king is righteousness”; Hebrews renders it “king of righteousness”. Salem sounds like shālôm, peace. Righteousness and peace are the gifts of the Messiah (Psalm 85:10).

Genesis gives Melchizedek no parents and no genealogy, unlike the priests of Levi, whose descent had to be proven. Hebrews reads the silence as a sign pointing to Christ, whose priesthood does not come by descent.
“Made like” the Son of God. Melchizedek is the copy; Christ is the original. The figure points forward to the one who fulfils it.
vv: Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.

The author reasons from what Scripture leaves unsaid, a known way of reading in his time. He is not saying Melchizedek was an angel or a heavenly being; he is saying the text has been shaped to point beyond him.
It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.
Abraham, the father of the people of the promise, bows to receive a blessing. The priesthood of Christ is greater than any priesthood before it.
In the one case, tithes are received by those who are mortal; in the other, by one of whom it is testified that he lives.
In Easter light the phrase points to Christ, who “always lives to make intercession” for us (7:25).
ch: The Catechism says that Christian tradition sees Melchizedek, “priest of God Most High”, as a figure of the priesthood of Christ (CCC 1544), and that the Church sees in his offering of bread and wine a prefiguring of her own offering (CCC 1333). St Cyprian, writing on the cup of the Lord, saw in Melchizedek's bread and wine an image of the Eucharistic sacrifice (in substance). Every priest who offers the Holy Qurbana stands within the one priesthood of Christ, which is not passed on by birth but given by the Lord.

set: Jesus has healed a man at the pool of Bethzatha on a sabbath and has called God his own Father. In John's language “the Jews” who start to persecute him (5:16–18) are the religious authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people; the healed man, the disciples and Jesus himself were Jews.
Jesus now speaks as one on trial. Under the Law a matter was settled by the evidence of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), so he brings his witnesses.
str: v. 30: the Son does nothing on his own; he seeks the Father's will.
vv. 31–32: self-testimony is not enough; there is another witness.
vv. 33–35: John the Baptist, the burning and shining lamp.
v. 36: the works that the Father gave him.
vv. 37–38: the Father himself, whose word they do not keep.
kw: A key word of John's Gospel. The whole Gospel is presented as testimony so that the reader may believe (19:35; 20:31).
John the Baptist is a lamp, lit from another flame. The Prologue says “He himself was not the light, but he came to testify to the light” (1:8). Jesus is the light itself.
John's word for the signs and deeds of Jesus. They are works the Father has given him “to complete”, a verb from the same root as “It is finished” on the Cross (19:30).
vv: I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge; and my judgment is just, because I seek to do not my own will but the will of him who sent me.
The Son is never independent of the Father. This is not weakness but the deepest unity.
He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.
“For a while”: interest in a good preacher can fade. A lamp is meant to lead us to the light.
The works that the Father has given me to complete, the very works that I am doing, testify on my behalf that the Father has sent me.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the signs worked by Jesus attest that the Father has sent him and invite belief in him (CCC 548). The greatest of the Father's testimonies is the Resurrection, by which he raised his Son. The Church in her turn is a witness: the apostles bore testimony to the Risen One, and every baptized person is sent to do the same.

qa: Was Melchizedek a real person, or Christ himself appearing in the Old Testament?

Genesis presents him as a real king of Salem, which tradition identifies with Jerusalem. A few ancient writers thought he was a heavenly figure, but the mainstream of the Church's tradition reads him as a man whom Scripture describes in a way that makes him a figure of Christ. Hebrews says he “resembles” the Son of God; it does not say he is the Son.
study: John the Baptist was a lamp that pointed beyond himself. Whom does my life point to?
Which “works” of God in my own life bear witness to me that the Father has sent his Son?

lead: Both readings ask what makes teaching true. Second Peter warns that false teachers will arise inside the community, as false prophets arose in Israel, and that they will deny the Master who bought them. In Matthew, Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem question Jesus about washing hands, and he answers with Isaiah's word about honour given with the lips while the heart is far away. True teaching hands on what God has given and leads to a true heart. The key words are heresy, tradition and heart.

set: Second Peter is written as Peter's farewell testament (1:13–15). Many scholars think it comes from a later generation that wrote in his name to keep his teaching alive, while others defend Peter's own authorship; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. Chapter 2 is closely related to the short Letter of Jude.

The letter has just spoken of the prophetic word, which comes not by human will but from the Holy Spirit (1:20–21). Now it turns to the shadow side: in Israel there were false prophets, and in the Church there will be false teachers.
str: v. 1: false teachers will arise; they bring in destructive opinions and deny the Master.
v. 2: many will follow them, and the way of truth will be maligned.
v. 3: their greed and deceptive words; their judgment is not asleep.
kw: Hairesis first meant a choice or a party (Acts 5:17 uses it of the Sadducees). Here it already means a chosen opinion that cuts a person off from the common faith, the root of our word heresy.
The owner of a household and its slaves. The false teachers deny the very Lord who “bought” them at the price of his blood (compare 1 Corinthians 6:20).
Literally “moulded words”, shaped like clay to fit what the hearers want. Our word plastic comes from the same root.
vv: just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive opinions.
The danger is inside, not outside, and it comes “secretly”: a gradual shift rather than open denial.
because of these teachers the way of truth will be maligned.
Acts calls the Christian faith “the Way” (Acts 9:2). Bad lives among believers bring shame on the faith in the eyes of others.
And in their greed they will exploit you with deceptive words.
The verb means to trade in people, to make merchandise of them. Faith turned into business is a temptation in every age.
ch: The Catechism defines heresy as the obstinate denial, after baptism, of a truth which must be believed with divine and catholic faith (CCC 2089). It is distinct from honest questions and doubts. The Church's teaching office does not stand above the word of God but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on (CCC 86). Against “moulded words” the faithful have the Creed, which the Church professes in every Holy Qurbana.

r.h: Honour with the lips, and the heart far away
set: A delegation of Pharisees and scribes comes from Jerusalem to Galilee. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to living the Law in daily life; many scholars think they wished to bring the holiness of the Temple to every table, which is why they washed hands before meals. Their “tradition of the elders” was the oral teaching that applied the Law to daily life.

Jesus does not attack the Law. He points to a case where a human custom was used to escape a commandment of God. Matthew's account is close to Mark 7, without Mark's explanation of the washing customs for non-Jewish readers.
str: vv. 1–2: the charge: your disciples break the tradition of the elders.
vv. 3–6: Jesus' counter-question: you break the commandment of God; the example of a gift dedicated to God.
vv. 7–9: Isaiah's prophecy: lips and heart.
kw: Something handed on. The word is neutral: Paul praises the Corinthians for keeping the traditions he handed on (1 Corinthians 11:2). The question is whether a tradition serves God's word or empties it.

Mark gives the Aramaic word korban, “an offering” (Mark 7:11). A son could declare his goods dedicated to God and then refuse them to his parents. Jewish teachers themselves discussed such vows and how they could be released.
In Greek, an actor on the stage. Jesus uses it for those whose outward religion does not match the heart.
vv: And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?
For God said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’
The fourth commandment (Exodus 20:12). Jesus defends the care of aged parents against a pious excuse.
This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me;
Isaiah 29:13, quoted in the Greek form. It is a prophet's word to his own people, and like all prophecy it is addressed to the people of God in every age, the Church included.
ch: The Catechism distinguishes the Tradition that comes from the apostles, handing on what they received from Christ, from the many theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions that arise in local Churches; these can be kept, changed or dropped under the guidance of the Church's teaching office (CCC 83). Jesus' rebuke is therefore no reason to despise Tradition. It is a warning that any custom, ours included, can be used to avoid love. The fourth commandment asks grown children to give their parents material and moral support in old age (CCC 2218).

qa: Is Jesus saying here that the Pharisees were hypocrites in general?

No. He answers a particular dispute with a particular example, as the prophets did. Many Pharisees were devout, and some were friends of Jesus and of the early Church (Luke 13:31; Acts 5:34; 15:5). The warning about lips and heart is for every believer, and the Church reads it first as a word to herself.
study: Is there a custom or excuse in my life that keeps me from caring for my parents or elders?
When I pray or sing in the Holy Qurbana, where is my heart?

lead: Ephesians calls the sleeper to rise from the dead so that Christ may shine on him, and then describes a community filled with the Spirit, singing and giving thanks to the Father at all times. Mark shows a crowd in a deserted place at evening, and Jesus who takes five loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks and gives. Both readings end at a table of thanksgiving, the table the Church sets in every Holy Qurbana. The key words are light, thanksgiving and broken bread.

set: The second half of Ephesians turns from God's plan in Christ to the life that follows from it. Just before this passage the letter contrasts the works of darkness with life as “children of light” (5:8). Ephesians presents itself as Paul's; many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name, while others hold that it is Paul's own.

Verse 14 introduces a quotation with “Therefore it says”, but the words are not found in the Old Testament. Many scholars think they come from an early Christian hymn sung at baptism, when the newly baptized came up from the water into the light.
str: vv. 13–14: what the light exposes becomes light; the baptismal call to rise.
vv. 15–17: live wisely; make the most of the time.
v. 18: not drunk with wine, but filled with the Spirit.
vv. 19–21: psalms and hymns, thanksgiving at all times, mutual submission.
kw: The verb is used of the dawn. Christ comes on the sleeper as the sun rises on the world. The early Church called baptism “enlightenment” (compare Hebrews 6:4).
making the most of the time
Literally “buying up the opportune moment”, as a merchant buys up goods while they are available. Each day holds chances for good that will not come again.
A command in the present tense: keep on being filled. Being filled with the Spirit is not a single event but a way of life.
vv: Sleeper, awake! Rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.

Clement of Alexandria knew a longer form of this hymn, which goes on to speak of Christ as the Sun of the Resurrection (in substance). In the season of the Resurrection we hear it as our own baptismal call.
Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery; but be filled with the Spirit,
At Pentecost some onlookers thought the apostles were drunk (Acts 2:13). The Spirit gives a joy that does not come from a cup.
giving thanks to God the Father at all times and for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The Greek verb is eucharisteō, from which the word Eucharist comes.
ch: The Church's sung liturgy takes up this passage: psalms, hymns and spiritual songs addressed to the Father through Christ in the Spirit. The Catechism teaches that singing and music serve the liturgy when they express prayer, unite the assembly and give solemnity to the celebration (CCC 1157). Thanksgiving “at all times and for everything” is the spirit of the Holy Qurbana, the great thanksgiving of the Church. Verse 21 opens the passage on Christian households that follows; all its instructions stand under mutual reverence for Christ.

set: The apostles have returned from their first mission, and Jesus has taken them to a deserted place to rest. A great crowd follows, and he has compassion on them, “because they were like sheep without a shepherd” (6:34), recalling Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34. He teaches them, and now it is late.
Apart from the Resurrection, this is the only miracle of Jesus told in all four Gospels. John adds that the Passover was near (John 6:4), which fits Mark's “green grass” of spring.
str: vv. 35–36: the disciples' practical advice: send them away.
vv. 37–38: “You give them something to eat”; five loaves and two fish.
vv. 39–40: the crowd seated in groups on the green grass.
v. 41: the blessing and the breaking.
vv. 42–44: all are filled; twelve baskets; five thousand men.
kw: The wilderness recalls Israel fed with manna (Exodus 16). God feeds his people where nothing grows.
The Jewish blessing over bread praises God who brings forth bread from the earth. Jesus takes, blesses, breaks and gives, the same four actions as at the Last Supper (Mark 14:22).
The word for the fragments. The Didache, a very early Christian writing, uses the same word for the bread broken at the Eucharist (Didache 9).
vv: You give them something to eat.
The disciples see a problem to send away; Jesus sees people to feed, and he makes his disciples part of the answer.
Then he ordered them to get all the people to sit down in groups on the green grass.
Mark says literally “table-groups, table-groups”. Many hear Psalm 23 here: the shepherd makes his flock lie down in green pastures and spreads a table.
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, and blessed and broke the loaves, and gave them to his disciples to set before the people;
He gives through the disciples. The Lord still feeds his people through the hands of those he sends.
and they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish.
Twelve, the number of the tribes of Israel and of the apostles. There is more than enough.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord says the blessing, breaks and distributes the loaves through his disciples to feed the multitude, prefigures the superabundance of the one bread of his Eucharist (CCC 1335). The Holy Qurbana is this table: the Lord's compassion for the hungry, his blessing to the Father, his body broken and given through the hands of his ministers. And the command “You give them something to eat” sends the Church to the hungry of the world.

qa: Was the multiplication a real miracle, or only the crowd sharing what they had brought?

All four Gospels present it as a miracle worked by Jesus, and the Church reads it so. The idea that the crowd simply shared their food is a modern explanation that the texts do not support. The sign is real, and it points beyond itself to the Bread of Life.
study: Where is the Lord saying to me, “You give them something to eat”?
Ephesians asks for thanks “at all times and for everything”. For what do I find it hardest to give thanks?

lead: Today the Church keeps Mar Geevarghese Sahada, St George the Martyr, a soldier who, tradition says, chose Christ above his career and his life in the persecution under Diocletian. The four readings of the feast are four pictures of faithful witness under threat. Daniel keeps praying to his God although a royal decree forbids it, and God shuts the lions' mouths. In Acts, King Herod kills James with the sword and imprisons Peter, and the Church prays. Paul, pressed by a thorn in the flesh, hears the Lord say, “My grace is sufficient for you”. In Matthew, Jesus asks to be loved above all, and promises that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it.

The calendar gives longer forms of these readings (Acts 12:1–23; 2 Corinthians 12:1–14; Matthew 10:37–42 with 16:24–27 and 19:29–30). The weekday readings of the Fourth Saturday are 1 Corinthians 14:20–25 and Mark 6:1–6. In the Latin calendar St George was kept on 23 April. Sahada is Syriac for witness, martyr. The key words are witness, prayer, weakness and worthy.

r.h: Daniel in the den of lions
set: The first half of the Book of Daniel tells stories of Jewish exiles who stay faithful at the court of foreign kings. Chapter 6 is set under “Darius the Mede”, a king not known from other ancient sources; many scholars think the book reached its final form in the second century BC, when the Jewish people suffered under the Syrian king Antiochus IV, and that these stories were told to strengthen those who were being forced to give up their faith. Whatever its literary form, the Church reads the book as inspired Scripture.

Envious officials have persuaded the king to sign a decree that for thirty days no one may pray to any god or man except the king. Daniel goes home, opens his windows toward Jerusalem, and prays three times a day “just as he had done previously” (6:10). This chapter, like most of Daniel 2–7, is written in Aramaic.
str: vv. 12–13: the accusation: Daniel prays three times a day.
vv. 14–15: the king's distress; the law that cannot be changed.
vv. 16–18: Daniel thrown to the lions; the stone and the seal; the king's sleepless night.
vv. 19–22: at dawn: “has your God been able to deliver you?” “My God sent his angel.”
vv. 23–24: Daniel taken up unharmed; the accusers punished.
kw: A binding prohibition. Its weakness is that it cannot be changed even when the king who signed it wants to. Human law that refuses God is shown to be a trap for the very ruler who makes it.
The lions' pit, closed with a stone and sealed. Christian readers have long seen in it a picture of the sealed tomb (Matthew 27:66), from which the servant of God comes out alive at dawn.
The king's own words (v. 20). Daniel's God is not an image or a decree; he acts. Hebrews remembers those who “shut the mouths of lions” by faith (Hebrews 11:33).
vv: May your God, whom you faithfully serve, deliver you!
The king's helpless prayer is the first sign that Daniel's faithfulness has already won his heart.
Then, at break of day, the king got up and hurried to the den of lions.
The hour of dawn, and a hurried visit to a sealed pit: Christians cannot hear this without thinking of the women at the tomb on Easter morning.
My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths so that they would not hurt me,
no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.
The reason is stated plainly: trust. Not every martyr is delivered from the lions, as St George was not; but every one who trusts is held by God, in life and in death.
The king gave a command, and those who had accused Daniel were brought and thrown into the den of lions

The ancient story ends with a harsh punishment, which also falls on the accusers' wives and children. The Law itself forbids putting children to death for their parents' sins (Deuteronomy 24:16), and the Gospel asks us to pray for our persecutors (Matthew 5:44). We read this ending as part of an old tale, not as a model.
ch: Daniel among the lions is one of the scenes most often painted in the catacombs of Rome: the first Christians, themselves thrown to beasts, saw in him the promise of God's faithfulness and of the resurrection. St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to die in the arena, wrote to the Romans: “I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, that I may be found pure bread of Christ” (Letter to the Romans 4). The Church reads Daniel as a witness that the faithful must obey God rather than any human power that commands what God forbids (compare Acts 5:29).

r.h: James is killed; the Church prays for Peter
set: “King Herod” here is Herod Agrippa I, a grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea from AD 41 to 44. Acts tells of his sudden death a little later in the chapter (12:20–23). The killing of James can therefore be dated to about AD 44.

Luke writes that Herod saw “that it pleased the Jews”. He means the circles in Jerusalem whose favour the king was seeking at that time, not the Jewish people as a whole; Peter, James and the whole Jerusalem church were themselves Jews. As the Church refuses to blame the Jewish people as a whole for the Passion of Christ (CCC 597), so she does not blame them for the sufferings of the apostles.
str: v. 1: Herod begins to persecute members of the church.
v. 2: James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.
vv. 3–4: Peter arrested at the festival of Unleavened Bread and guarded by four squads.
v. 5: Peter kept in prison; the church prays fervently.
kw: James is killed with the sword, most likely beheaded, as tradition says St George would be. Jesus had told James and John, “You will indeed drink my cup” (Matthew 20:23). James is the first of the Twelve whose martyrdom the New Testament records.
Four squads of four soldiers, taking turns through the night. Luke shows how strongly Peter is held, so that his rescue in the verses that follow is plainly God's work.
Stretched out, earnest. Luke uses a form of the same word for the prayer of Jesus in his agony (Luke 22:44, a verse found in many manuscripts).
vv: He had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.
A single verse for the death of an apostle. Luke does not dwell on it; the witness is given, and the Gospel goes on.
(This was during the festival of Unleavened Bread.)
Peter is arrested at Passover time, as his Lord was. The disciple's way follows the Master's.
While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him.
This is the Church's answer to persecution. She does not have swords or soldiers; she prays.
ch: The Church has always prayed for those in prison for their faith and for those who suffer persecution in many lands. In Acts she prays for Peter, and the Church still prays especially for the successor of Peter. The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473), and it speaks of the Church gathering the records of those who have gone to the end to bear witness to their faith (CCC 2474). We pray also for those who persecute, as Christ and the martyrs did.

set: In chapters 10–13 Paul answers rivals in Corinth whom he calls, with irony, “super-apostles” (11:5). They boasted of their visions and their eloquence. Paul reluctantly enters a “fool's speech” (11:16–12:13): if he must boast, he will boast of what shows his weakness, his beatings, shipwrecks and dangers (11:23–29).

Now he speaks of a vision fourteen years before, which would place it in the early 40s, before his great missionary journeys. He speaks of himself in the third person, as “a person in Christ”, as if the experience were too great to claim as his own.
str: vv. 1–4: the man caught up to the third heaven, into Paradise.
vv. 5–6: Paul will boast only of his weaknesses.
v. 7: the thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan.
vv. 8–9a: three times he asks; the Lord answers.
vv. 9b–10: “when I am weak, then I am strong”.
kw: A Persian word for a walled garden. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the garden of Eden, and Jesus promises it to the thief on the cross (Luke 23:43).

A stake or sharp splinter. Paul does not say what it was. St John Chrysostom understood it of the opponents and persecutions that troubled Paul (in substance); others have thought of an illness, perhaps the one he mentions in Galatians 4:13. The Church has never settled it, and the lesson is the same either way.
Enough. The Lord does not remove the thorn; he promises enough grace to carry it.
Literally “may pitch a tent upon”. The power of Christ comes to rest on Paul's weakness as the glory of God rested on the tent in the wilderness.
vv: Therefore, to keep me from being too elated, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me,
“Was given”: Paul sees God's hand even in what Satan uses to torment him.
Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me,
Three times, like Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 14:32–41). It is right to ask for healing. The answer may come in another form than the one we asked for.
My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.
Paul seldom quotes words the risen Lord spoke to him personally; here he does. The verb “said” is in the Greek perfect tense: a word given once and still standing.
Therefore I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities for the sake of Christ; for whenever I am weak, then I am strong.
“For the sake of Christ” is what gives the sufferings their meaning. Weakness in itself is not strength; weakness handed over to Christ becomes the place of his power.
ch: The Catechism teaches that only faith can embrace the mysterious ways of God's almighty power, and that this faith glories in its weaknesses in order to draw to itself Christ's power (CCC 273). The martyrs prove it. Tradition remembers a soldier who would not save his life by denying Christ, and was put to death; and the Church, centuries later, still calls him victorious. In every age the sick, the persecuted and the poor who hold to Christ are a sign of this power made perfect in weakness.

r.h: Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it
set: Matthew 10 is the second of the five great discourses in his Gospel: Jesus sends out the Twelve and tells them what to expect. He has just warned them of persecution, of trials before governors and kings, and of division even inside families (10:16–36).

These verses end the discourse. They begin with the cost of discipleship and end with the reward of those who receive the disciples. Luke has a harsher form of the first saying: whoever does not “hate” father and mother (Luke 14:26), a Semitic way of saying “love less”. Matthew gives the meaning: love more than me.
str: v. 37: love for Christ above father, mother, son and daughter.
v. 38: taking up the cross.
v. 39: losing and finding one's life.
v. 40: whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and the one who sent me.
vv. 41–42: the reward of welcoming a prophet, a righteous person, a little one.
kw: Worth as much as. Said three times in vv. 37–38. Nothing earns this worthiness; it is a matter of what we place first.
The disciples knew the cross as the Roman punishment for rebels and slaves. In Matthew the saying comes before Jesus speaks of his own cross; after Easter the Church heard it as a call to share his.
Life, self, soul. To keep one's life for oneself is to lose it; to give it for Christ is to find it in him.
To take someone in as a guest. Jewish teaching said that a person's agent is like the one who sends him; Jesus applies this to his messengers.
vv: Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me;
Only God can rightly ask this. Jesus speaks with the authority of the God who commanded Israel to love him with all the heart (Deuteronomy 6:5).
and whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.
Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.
This is one of the sayings the Gospels repeat most often (compare 16:25). The martyr is its clearest proof.
whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple
The smallest act of kindness to a disciple is not forgotten. Not everyone is called to martyrdom, but everyone can welcome and help those who suffer for Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that martyrdom is the supreme witness to the truth of the faith: the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity (CCC 2473). Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is seed (Apology 50, in substance). St George is honoured as one who heard this Gospel and did it: he loved Christ more than his own life, and he found it. The saying about the cup of cold water reminds us that the Church honours the martyrs also by caring for those who suffer for their faith today.

qa: Did St George really kill a dragon?

No. The story of the dragon appears many centuries after his death, in the Middle Ages, and it is a legend, not history. What history gives us is small but solid: a martyr honoured at his tomb at Lydda from the early centuries. The Church reads the dragon as a picture of a truth: the martyr's faith overcomes the ancient serpent (Revelation 12:9–11).
Why was James killed and Peter rescued?

Acts does not explain it, and we should not try to. Both were faithful; both belonged to the Lord. Peter too would later give his life in Rome. God's ways with each of his servants are his own, and the Church honours the one who died and the one who was spared, as Daniel was.
Does Jesus set himself against love of family?

No. He commands us to honour father and mother (Matthew 15:4; 19:19). He asks to be loved first, and love of family is then held within love of him. When a family demands that we deny Christ, as St George's world demanded of him, then Christ must come first.
rite: In the Syriac tradition martyrs are called sahde, witnesses, and George is Mar Geevarghese Sahada. Early in this season, on the Friday after the feast of the Resurrection, the Syro-Malabar Church kept the feast of all the holy martyrs; today she honours one of the best-loved among them. Kerala is full of his churches and his name, and great pilgrim churches such as Aruvithura and Edathua draw crowds who come with their fears and their vows. The readings ask us not only to seek his help but to share his choice: Christ first.
study: Daniel kept praying as he had done before, decree or no decree. What daily prayer of mine would I keep if it became costly?
The Church prayed fervently for Peter. Whom should I pray for who suffers for the faith?
Where in my life might the Lord be saying, “My grace is sufficient for you”?
What do I love more than Christ, and what would it mean to put him first?

lead: This Sunday bears the name of Mar Addai, the apostle of Edessa, and its four readings move from darkness into light and from a long night to a meal at dawn. Isaiah hears God say to prisoners, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Show yourselves.” In Acts a light from heaven throws Saul to the ground, and the persecutor is led by the hand, blind, into Damascus, where his new life will begin. Hebrews tells the baptized that a new and living way into God’s presence stands open, and that they must not stay away from the assembly. In John the risen Lord stands on the shore after a night of empty nets, fills the net, and feeds his disciples with bread and fish. The words to watch are light, way and Lord. The feast of St Mark the Evangelist (25 April) gives way to the Sunday this year.

set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ. Many scholars think they come from a prophet of the exile who stands in the tradition of Isaiah of Jerusalem. The message is consolation: God is about to bring his people home in a new exodus.

Just before this reading comes the second of the four “Servant songs” (49:1–6), in which the Servant, called “Israel” (49:3), is made “a light to the nations”. Today’s verses take up that Servant, despised and enslaved, and promise that kings will bow before him. Then the road home opens.
str: v. 7: the one deeply despised will be honoured by kings.
vv. 8–9a: a day of salvation: the Servant given as a covenant, prisoners called out.
vv. 9b–11: the new exodus: pasture on bare heights, springs of water, mountains made into a road.
v. 12: the scattered come from every direction.
v. 13: heaven, earth and mountains are called to sing.
kw: A moment chosen by God’s good pleasure. It is not a time we fix; it is the time God gives.
The Servant does not only make a covenant; he is the covenant (also 42:6). Christians hear this fulfilled in the one who says, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (1 Corinthians 11:25).

The verb behind “he who has pity on them” (v. 10) and “will have compassion” (v. 13) is related to reḥem, the womb. Two verses later God asks, “Can a woman forget her nursing child?” (49:15). God’s compassion is a mother’s love.
vv: Thus says the Lord, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nations, the slave of rulers,
The despised one and the exalted one are the same. The Church has always read here the way of Christ, rejected and then raised, which the fourth Servant song (52:13–53:12) will tell in full.
In a time of favor I have answered you, on a day of salvation I have helped you;
St Paul quotes this verse and adds, “See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!” (2 Corinthians 6:2). The day Isaiah promised is today.
saying to the prisoners, “Come out,” to those who are in darkness, “Show yourselves.”
Read beside today’s second reading, this verse describes Saul: in darkness three days, then called out into the light.
they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them down, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them.
The Book of Revelation takes up these words for the great multitude before the throne, whom the Lamb will guide “to springs of the water of life” (Revelation 7:16–17).
and these from the land of Syene.
Textual note: the traditional Hebrew text reads “the land of Sinim”. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran supports “Syene”, the town of Aswan on the southern border of Egypt, and the NRSV follows it.
ch: The Church reads the Servant of these songs as Christ. The Catechism says that the Messiah’s characteristics are revealed above all in the Servant songs, which proclaim the meaning of Jesus’ Passion (CCC 713). Simeon greets the child Jesus as “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32), and Paul and Barnabas take up Isaiah 49:6 for their own mission to the nations (Acts 13:47). Jewish readers have understood the Servant as Israel, as the song itself names him (49:3), and we read that with respect: the Church confesses that Christ takes up and fulfils the calling of Israel, which God has never revoked (Romans 11:29).

r.h: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
set: After the death of Stephen, at which Saul stood by and approved (8:1), a persecution scattered the believers of Jerusalem. Saul, a Pharisee and zealous for the law (Philippians 3:5–6), now carries the campaign to Damascus, where there were synagogues and already some disciples of Jesus.

Acts tells this event three times: here, and twice in Paul’s own speeches (22:6–16; 26:12–18). Luke never mentions a horse; that comes from later painting. Everyone in the scene is Jewish: Saul, the high priest, the disciples in Damascus, and Jesus himself. This is a quarrel within one people over Jesus, not a story of Jews against Christians.
str: vv. 1–2: Saul’s plan and the letters from the high priest.
vv. 3–4: light from heaven, the fall, the voice.
vv. 5–6: “Who are you, Lord?” “I am Jesus.” The command to go into the city.
vv. 7–9: the companions; three days blind, without food or drink.
kw: The earliest name of the Christian movement in Acts (also 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14). Before they were called Christians, the disciples were people of a road: the way of the one who said, “I am the way” (John 14:6).
The voice uses this verb twice. Saul thought he was pursuing men and women; he was pursuing Christ.

Here the Greek keeps the Hebrew form of his name, not the Greek form Saulos. In 26:14 Paul says the voice spoke “in the Hebrew language”. The name is doubled, as God called “Abraham, Abraham” and “Samuel! Samuel!”
vv: He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”

Saul had never met Jesus in Galilee. He had seized his disciples. Yet the Lord says “me”. Here, at the very beginning of Paul’s life as an apostle, is the seed of his later teaching: “you are the body of Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:27).
“Who are you, Lord?” The reply came, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
The question of a man whose certainty has fallen with him. The answer is a name: Jesus, alive.
though his eyes were open, he could see nothing; so they led him by the hand
The man who came to lead others away in chains is himself led by the hand. His blindness is not a punishment but a pause, until another disciple, Ananias, lays hands on him (9:17).
For three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
Three days of darkness and fasting, and then light and baptism (9:18). Many readers see here Saul’s own share in the three days of the Lord’s death and rising.
ch: St Augustine often returns to this voice from heaven. Christ, he says, was seated in heaven and no one could touch him there, yet he cried out “Why do you persecute me?”, because the head speaks for the members, and Christ and his Church are one (in substance). The Catechism takes up Augustine’s teaching on the “whole Christ”, head and members (CCC 795). Paul himself never forgot what he had been: “I am the least of the apostles, unfit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God” (1 Corinthians 15:9). The Church does not pray for her persecutors as enemies to be destroyed but as people Christ may still call.

set: The Letter to the Hebrews does not name its author. In the early centuries some thought it was by Paul and some did not; today most scholars think it comes from a teacher close to Paul’s circle. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture whoever its writer was.

Chapters 7–10 have shown that Christ is the true high priest. Once a year the high priest of Israel passed behind the curtain into the Holy of Holies with blood (9:7). Christ has entered the true sanctuary once for all. Today’s reading begins the great “therefore”: what we are to do now that the way is open.
str: vv. 19–21: two reasons: we have confidence to enter, and we have a great priest.
v. 22: “let us approach”: faith.
v. 23: “let us hold fast”: hope.
vv. 24–25: “let us consider how to provoke one another”: love, shown in the assembly. ¶ Faith, hope and love, the three that Paul names together (1 Corinthians 13:13), give the passage its shape.
kw: Literally the right to speak openly, the boldness of a citizen with full rights. Through the blood of Jesus we stand before God as children, not as strangers.
The veil before the Holy of Holies. The Gospels say it was torn in two when Jesus died (Mark 15:38). Hebrews says the true curtain is his flesh: we pass to God through the body of Christ.

The gathering of the community (v. 25). The same noun is used in 2 Thessalonians 2:1 for our being gathered to the Lord at his coming. Every Sunday assembly is a small foretaste of that last gathering.
vv: by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain (that is, through his flesh),
The way is not a method but a person. It is “new” because it was never open before, and “living” because the one who opened it is alive.
our bodies washed with pure water.
Many commentators, ancient and modern, hear Baptism in these words, joined to the sprinkling of the heart. The way into the sanctuary begins at the font.
Let us hold fast to the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who has promised is faithful.
Our firmness rests on God’s faithfulness, not on our own strength. Christian assurance is a hope, held fast.
not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some,
Already in the first generation some were drifting away from the assembly. The remedy given is not a rule alone but mutual encouragement.
ch: The Catechism cites this verse when it teaches that the practice of the Christian assembly goes back to the beginnings of the apostolic age (CCC 2178). St John Paul II’s letter on keeping Sunday holy, Dies Domini (1998), presents the Sunday Eucharist as the heart of the Christian week. In Hebrews the one sacrifice of Christ is never repeated, and in the Holy Qurbana it is not repeated but made present, so that the assembly enters the sanctuary by the same new and living way.

set: John 20 seems to close the Gospel: “these are written so that you may come to believe” (20:31). Chapter 21 then adds one more appearance. Many scholars think it was added by the evangelist’s disciples, who say “we know that his testimony is true” (21:24). No ancient manuscript of the Gospel lacks it, and the Church receives it as part of the inspired Gospel.

The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee, named after the city Herod Antipas built on its shore. Seven disciples are there, among them Thomas, the apostle our Church calls its father in faith. They go back to the work they knew. Night was the usual time for fishing on the lake.
str: vv. 1–3: seven disciples, Peter’s decision, a night with nothing.
vv. 4–6: a stranger on the shore at daybreak; the net cast on the right side.
vv. 7–8: the beloved disciple recognizes him; Peter leaps into the sea.
vv. 9–11: the charcoal fire, the bread and fish; one hundred fifty-three large fish; the net not torn.
vv. 12–14: “Come and have breakfast”; he gives them bread and fish; the third appearance.
kw: A tender word (v. 5), the address of a father or an elder to those in his care. The one who asks has the meal already prepared.

This word appears in the New Testament only here and in 18:18, where Peter warmed himself and denied the Lord. Peter is brought back to a charcoal fire, and in the next verses he will be asked three times, “Do you love me?”
From schizō, the root of “schism”. At the Cross the soldiers said of Jesus’ tunic, “Let us not tear it” (19:24), using the same verb. The net of the Church holds many and is not torn.
vv: Just after daybreak, Jesus stood on the beach; but the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.
In John’s Easter stories the Risen Lord is not at once recognized: by Mary Magdalene in the garden (20:14), and now by these fishermen. He is the same Lord, but recognizing him is a gift.
That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!”
Love sees first; Peter acts first. The beloved disciple and Peter appear together at the empty tomb as well (20:3–8). The Church needs both.
full of large fish, a hundred fifty-three of them; and though there were so many, the net was not torn.
The exact number shows that someone counted. The Fathers saw in it a sign of the fullness of the Church (see below).
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and did the same with the fish.
These are the movements of the feeding of the five thousand by the same lake (6:11). The early Christians could not hear them without thinking of the Eucharist.
ch: St Augustine notes that 153 is the sum of all the numbers from 1 to 17, and that seventeen joins the ten commandments of the law to the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit; the number stands for all who are saved by grace (in substance, Tractates on John 122). St Jerome reports that writers on fishes counted a hundred and fifty-three kinds, so the full net shows the Church gathering every kind of people (in substance). The Catechism points to this meal when it says that the Risen Lord established direct contact with his disciples by the sharing of a meal (CCC 645).

qa: Why did the disciples not recognize Jesus at once?

The Risen Lord is truly the same Jesus, in the same body that bore the wounds, but that body is now glorified and no longer bound by the conditions of this life (CCC 645–646). In John’s Gospel recognition comes through a word or a sign: Mary knows him when he calls her name; the fishermen know him through the full net. Faith is needed to see him, then and now.
Acts 9:7 says Saul’s companions heard the voice, but Acts 22:9 says they did not hear it. Is this a contradiction?

Luke wrote both passages and saw no contradiction. One common explanation is that the companions heard a sound but did not understand the words spoken to Saul; the Greek verb for “hear” can carry both senses. In both accounts the point is the same: the others knew something had happened, but the call was for Saul.
Does the number 153 have a hidden meaning?

John does not explain it. The number may simply record an eyewitness memory of a catch so great that it was counted. The Fathers drew lessons from it about the fullness and unity of the Church, and the Church allows such readings as long as they serve the plain sense: the Lord’s mission gathers all, and the net does not tear.
rite: The Syro-Malabar calendar keeps Mar Addai on the Fifth Sunday of Resurrection. The historian Eusebius, writing early in the fourth century, records a tradition from the archives of Edessa that after the Ascension the apostle Thomas sent Thaddaeus, one of the Seventy, to heal King Abgar and preach in that city; the Syriac tradition calls him Addai. How much of the story is history is debated, but the memory of an apostolic mission to Edessa is ancient and dear to all the Churches of the East. Most of our Holy Qurbanas are prayed with the Anaphora of the Apostles Mar Addai and Mar Mari, one of the oldest Eucharistic prayers still in use.

Today’s Gospel fits the day well. Thomas is in the boat; the Lord gives bread with his own hands; and Hebrews calls us to the assembly. When the sanctuary veil is drawn back and the Qurbana begins, we stand where the disciples stood on the shore: before the Lord who has already prepared the meal and asks us to bring some of our own catch.
study: Isaiah hears God say to prisoners, “Come out.” What darkness in my life, or in my family, needs that word today?
The Lord tells Saul that to persecute his disciples is to persecute him. How does this change the way I treat other Christians, and those who suffer for their faith?
Hebrews joins faith, hope and love to the Sunday assembly. Who in my circle has drifted from the Qurbana, and how could I encourage them?
The disciples worked all night and caught nothing until the Lord spoke. Where am I working hard without listening to him?

lead: Both readings speak of suffering and judgment, and both point to the Resurrection. Peter tells Christians not to be surprised by the fiery ordeal, because to share Christ’s sufferings is to share his glory. In Luke, Jesus refuses the crowd a sign on demand and offers only the sign of Jonah: a preacher whose word brought a pagan city to repentance. In this season we know what that sign became: the Son of Man given back from death.

r.h: Do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal
set: 1 Peter is written in Peter’s name from “Babylon” (5:13), a Christian code name for Rome, to believers scattered across Asia Minor (1:1). Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in Peter’s name after his death, others that it comes from Peter through Silvanus (5:12). Its readers suffer insults and pressure because they no longer share the life of their neighbours (4:4). The letter does not describe an organised empire-wide persecution, but the slow fire of being despised for Christ.
str: vv. 12–13: do not be surprised; rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings.
vv. 14–16: blessed if reviled for the name; but never suffer as a wrongdoer.
vv. 17–18: judgment begins with the household of God.
v. 19: entrust yourselves to a faithful Creator, and keep doing good.
kw: Literally a burning, the fire of the smelter. The letter has already said that faith is tested like gold in the fire (1:7). The fire purifies; it does not destroy.
One of only three places in the New Testament where the name appears (also Acts 11:26; 26:28). It was probably first a nickname given by outsiders. Peter tells believers to carry it with honour.
Only here in the New Testament is God called by this title. The one who made us will not abandon what he made.
vv: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal that is taking place among you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you.
Suffering for Christ is not a sign that something has gone wrong. The Master was treated so, and the disciple is not above the master.
But let none of you suffer as a murderer, a thief, a criminal, or even as a mischief maker.

An honest warning. Not every hardship a Christian meets is suffering for Christ; some comes from our own faults. The word translated “mischief maker” probably means a busybody who meddles in others’ affairs.
Therefore, let those suffering in accordance with God’s will entrust themselves to a faithful Creator, while continuing to do good.
The verb is the one Jesus used on the Cross: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). The Christian answer to unjust suffering is trust and continued goodness, not revenge.
ch: Verse 18 quotes Proverbs 11:31 in its Greek form. The Second Vatican Council teaches that martyrdom, by which the disciple is made like the Master, is regarded by the Church as an exceptional gift and the highest proof of love (Lumen Gentium 42). The Church today remembers that in many lands Christians still bear the name at great cost, and she prays for them and for those who wrong them.

r.h: Something greater than Jonah is here
set: Some in the crowd have just said that Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul, and others, to test him, asked for a sign from heaven (11:15–16). Jesus now answers that second group. The crowds are growing, but numbers are not faith.
str: v. 29: an evil generation asks for a sign; only the sign of Jonah will be given.
v. 30: as Jonah to Nineveh, so the Son of Man to this generation.
vv. 31–32: two witnesses from among the nations, the queen of the South and the people of Nineveh, will rise at the judgment.
kw: In Luke the sign is Jonah himself, a prophet whose preaching called to repentance. Matthew adds the three days and nights in the belly of the fish (Matthew 12:40), which makes the link to the Resurrection explicit.
Not a people or a race, but the people of a time who see and do not respond. The warning reaches every generation that hears the Gospel, ours included.
The Greek is neuter: not only “someone” but “something” greater. With Jesus the whole Kingdom of God has come near, greater than Solomon’s wisdom and Jonah’s preaching.
vv: it asks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.
Jesus will not perform on demand. The signs he gives call for conversion, not for applause.
The queen of the South will rise at the judgment with the people of this generation and condemn them,
The queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1–10) travelled far to hear Solomon. A foreign queen and a pagan city become the examples of openness. Those who seemed far away listened best.
they repented at the proclamation of Jonah, and see, something greater than Jonah is here!
Nineveh repented after one short sermon from a reluctant prophet (Jonah 3:4–5). How much more should we listen to the Son himself?
ch: The Fathers read the sign of Jonah as the Resurrection, following Matthew, and the Easter season gives this Gospel its full meaning: the greatest sign given to the world is the Son of Man risen from the dead. Our Syro-Malabar tradition holds the people of Nineveh in honour: before the Great Fast it keeps the three-day Rogation of the Ninevites, the Moonnu Nombu, asking for the same repentance that saved that city.

qa: Does Jesus condemn the Jewish people as an “evil generation”?

No. Jesus speaks as the prophets of Israel spoke, calling his own people to conversion, and the warning is addressed to all who hear and do not respond, in every age. The Church teaches that the Jewish people may not be presented as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598). The sign of Jonah is offered to us, and we are the generation now being asked.
study: When have I suffered because of my own faults, and when for Christ? How do I tell the difference?
The queen of the South travelled far to hear wisdom. What effort do I make to hear the word of the One greater than Solomon?

lead: Today’s readings ask for fruit. James warns against hearing the word and walking away unchanged, like a man who forgets his own face. In Matthew, Jesus finds a fig tree with leaves and no fruit, and then teaches the disciples the power of prayer made in faith. Leaves without fruit and hearing without doing are the same illness; the cure is faith that acts and prayer that trusts.

set: The Letter of James is a collection of practical teaching in the spirit of the wisdom books and of the Sermon on the Mount. It is addressed “to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” (1:1), probably Jewish Christians living outside the land of Israel. Tradition links it to James, “the brother of the Lord”, leader of the Church in Jerusalem. Just before today’s reading James has said, “welcome with meekness the implanted word that has the power to save your souls” (1:21).
str: vv. 22–24: hearers who forget, like a man before a mirror.
v. 25: the one who looks into the perfect law of liberty and perseveres.
vv. 26–27: worthless religion and pure religion.
kw: Not only listeners but people who carry the word out. In the Hebrew tradition, to hear (shema) already means to obey.
the perfect law, the law of liberty
For James the law, read in the light of Christ, does not enslave; it gives true liberty. He will soon call it “the royal law”: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (2:8).
The outward practice of worship. James does not despise it; he says that true worship shows itself in the care of the weak and in purity of life.
vv: But be doers of the word, and not merely hearers who deceive themselves.
The danger is self-deception: to feel good about having heard a sermon and to change nothing.
for they look at themselves and, on going away, immediately forget what they were like.
The word of God is a mirror that shows us our true face. A glance is not enough; we must look and stay.
Religion that is pure and undefiled before God, the Father, is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.
Orphans and widows were the most defenceless in ancient society, and the Law of Moses names God as their protector (Deuteronomy 10:18). Charity and holiness belong together.
ch: The Church has never set faith against works. The good works of a Christian are themselves the fruit of God’s grace, which we receive in faith and which works through us; that is why they can be pleasing to God (CCC 2008, 2011). James and Paul agree: Paul speaks of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem and cleansed the Temple (21:12–17). The next morning, on the road back from Bethany, the fig tree incident follows. Mark tells the story in two parts around the cleansing of the Temple and adds that “it was not the season for figs” (Mark 11:13); Matthew tells it in one scene and says the tree withered at once.
str: vv. 18–19: Jesus is hungry; a tree with leaves only; his word, and the tree withers.
v. 20: the disciples’ amazement.
vv. 21–22: the teaching on faith and prayer.
kw: The prophets used the fig tree as an image of God’s people and of the fruit God seeks (Jeremiah 8:13; Micah 7:1). The action is a prophetic sign, like those of Jeremiah and Ezekiel.
Literally “not be divided”, not torn between trust and distrust. James uses the same verb of the one who asks in prayer (James 1:6).
Not confidence in our own power, but trust in God to whom nothing is impossible.
vv: In the morning, when he returned to the city, he was hungry.
A small, human detail. The Son of God knew hunger, as he knew tiredness and thirst.
he went to it and found nothing at all on it but leaves.
Leaves promise fruit. The sign is a warning against any show of religion that bears no fruit: a warning to every disciple and every community, ours first.
Whatever you ask for in prayer with faith, you will receive.
This promise does not make God a servant of our wishes. Prayer in faith seeks first what God wills, and receives more than it asked (CCC 2610).
ch: The Church does not read the withered fig tree as a sentence on the Jewish people, whom God has never rejected (Romans 11:1–2, 29; CCC 839). The Fathers saw in it a lesson for every soul and every Church: God looks for fruit, not only leaves. The second half of the reading moves from judgment to hope: the disciples who have faith are promised that their prayer will be heard.

qa: Why would Jesus curse a tree for having no fruit?

The action is not a burst of anger at a plant. It is a prophetic sign, as when the prophets broke a jar or wore a yoke to make God’s word visible. Jesus uses the tree to teach what God seeks in his people: fruit, not appearance. The sign is a warning given in love, while there is still time to bear fruit.
study: What word from Scripture or a homily have I heard recently and not yet put into practice?
Where in my life are there leaves without fruit: signs of faith that are not yet matched by love?

lead: Both readings speak of a new birth and a new life. Colossians tells the baptized to put off the old self like a garment and put on the new, renewed in the image of the Creator, where Christ is all and in all. In John, Nicodemus comes by night and hears that no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit. The Easter season is the season of Baptism, and today’s readings explain what happened at the font.

set: The letter is written in the name of Paul to the Church at Colossae in Asia Minor. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple of Paul after his lifetime; others hold that Paul wrote it, perhaps through a co-worker. The Church reads it as part of the apostolic witness. Just before this reading the letter says, “you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (3:3). Today’s verses draw the consequences: because you have been raised with Christ, live accordingly.
str: vv. 5–7: put to death what is earthly: a first list of vices.
vv. 8–9a: get rid of sins of anger and the tongue: a second list.
vv. 9b–10: the old self stripped off, the new self put on.
v. 11: in the new creation the old divisions fall away: Christ is all and in all.
kw: A strong word. Baptism has already joined us to Christ’s death (2:12); now that death must be carried into daily life.
Literally “wanting more”. The letter calls it idolatry, because whatever we crave above God takes the place of God.
The language of changing clothes. Early Christian Baptism made it visible: the candidate took off old clothes, went down into the water, and was clothed in a white garment.
vv: Put to death, therefore, whatever in you is earthly:
“Earthly” does not mean the body or the material world, which God made good. It means the old life turned away from God.
On account of these the wrath of God is coming on those who are disobedient.
Textual note: the words “on those who are disobedient” are missing in some of the oldest manuscripts and may have come in from Ephesians 5:6. The POC follows the shorter text.
and have clothed yourselves with the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator.
An echo of Genesis 1:27. In Christ, the true image of God (1:15), the image in which we were made is restored.
In that renewal there is no longer Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave and free; but Christ is all and in all!
A “barbarian” was anyone who did not speak Greek; the Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were the byword for the uncivilized. None of these labels decides a person’s worth in Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Baptism makes the neophyte “a new creature”, an adopted son of God, a member of Christ (CCC 1265). The white garment given at Baptism, still part of our rite, shows that the baptized person has “put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27; CCC 1243). The conversion begun at the font continues through the whole Christian life (CCC 1428).

set: Nicodemus is a Pharisee and “a leader of the Jews”, a member of the ruling council. He comes by night, perhaps for safety, perhaps for quiet study; in John, night is also the darkness from which a person comes toward the light (3:19–21). He appears twice more: defending Jesus’ right to a hearing (7:50–51) and bringing spices for his burial (19:39). He is a man who slowly comes into the light.
str: vv. 1–2: Nicodemus comes by night: “we know that you are a teacher who has come from God.”
v. 3: Jesus: to see the kingdom, one must be born from above.
v. 4: Nicodemus misunderstands.
vv. 5–8: born of water and Spirit; flesh and spirit; the wind.
kw: The Greek means both. Jesus means “from above”, from God; Nicodemus hears “again”. Both are true: it is a second birth, and it comes from God. The POC renders it “again”.
The Church has always heard Baptism in these words: the water is the sign, the Spirit gives the life.
The same Greek word means both. Jesus plays on it in v. 8: you hear the wind and cannot see it; so it is with the Spirit and those born of him.
vv: He came to Jesus by night
He comes as a teacher to a teacher. He will learn that this is not a matter of better teaching but of new birth.
Very truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God without being born from above.
Jesus does not answer Nicodemus’s compliment; he answers his need.
Very truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit.
The Church’s classic text on the necessity of Baptism. God has bound salvation to Baptism, but he himself is not bound by his sacraments (CCC 1257).
So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.
The life of the Spirit cannot be controlled or predicted, but its effects can be seen, as the trees bend under the wind.
ch: The Catechism cites this Gospel when it explains that Baptism is called “the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit”, because it brings about the birth of water and the Spirit without which no one can enter the kingdom of God (CCC 1215). The Fathers delighted in the image of the font as the womb of Mother Church, where children are born of water and the Spirit.

study: Colossians names greed as idolatry. What do I want “more” of, so that it competes with God in my heart?
Nicodemus came by night and slowly came into the light. Where am I still coming to Jesus “by night”, privately and with caution?

lead: Hebrews hears the voice of the Holy Spirit in Psalm 95: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” John’s Gospel gives the voice that must be heard: the voice of the Son of God, which raises the spiritually dead now and will call all the dead from their graves at the last day. Today is also the memory of St Catherine of Siena (1347–1380), virgin and doctor of the Church; her own readings are 1 John 1:5–2:2 and Matthew 11:25–30. Few saints heard the Lord’s voice “today” with such readiness.

r.h: Today, if you hear his voice
set: Hebrews has just compared Moses, faithful as a servant in God’s house, with Christ, faithful as a Son over it (3:1–6). Now it quotes Psalm 95:7–11, a psalm Israel sang in worship, and applies it to Christians who are tempted to grow weary and drift away. The wilderness generation saw God’s works and still did not trust him; the readers are on their own journey to God’s rest.
str: vv. 7–11: the Holy Spirit speaks through the psalm: today, do not harden your hearts as in the wilderness.
v. 12: the warning: an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
v. 13: the remedy: exhort one another every day, while it is called today.
kw: The key word. The psalm’s “today” did not end in David’s time; it is renewed every time the word is proclaimed. God’s call is always for today, never to be put off until tomorrow.
In the Hebrew psalm these are place names, Meribah and Massah (Exodus 17:7). The Greek translates the names into their meaning, and Hebrews follows the Greek.
To make stiff or dry. A hardened heart is not one that cannot hear, but one that has heard and refused so often that it no longer responds.
vv: Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, “Today, if you hear his voice,
Hebrews does not say “as David said” or “as the psalm said”, but “as the Holy Spirit says”, in the present tense. Scripture is God speaking now.
where your ancestors put me to the test, though they had seen my works
Seeing great works does not by itself soften a heart. The wilderness generation had seen the sea divided and eaten manna.
Take care, brothers and sisters, that none of you may have an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
The danger is not first a wrong idea but a turning away. Unbelief here is a matter of the heart and the will.
But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,”
The cure for hardness is not solitary effort but the community. Christians are responsible for one another’s faith.
ch: The Catechism teaches that faith is a personal act, but not an isolated one: we believe within the Church, supported by the faith of others (CCC 166). Psalm 95 opens the daily prayer of many Churches. Its “today” is the voice of the Spirit to every generation, calling us to listen while there is time.

set: Jesus has healed a man on the Sabbath at the pool of Bethesda (5:1–9), and some of the authorities in Jerusalem object, since he calls God his own Father (5:18). Where John says “the Jews” in this chapter, he means these authorities; Jesus and his disciples were themselves Jews. Jesus answers with a long discourse on the Son, who does what the Father does: gives life and judges.
str: v. 24: whoever hears and believes has eternal life now.
vv. 25–27: the hour is now here: the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God; the Son has life in himself and authority to judge.
vv. 28–29: the hour is coming: all in the graves will hear his voice and come out.
kw: A perfect tense: the passage from death to life has already happened for the one who believes. Eternal life begins now, in faith and Baptism.
Both “now here” (v. 25) and “coming” (v. 28). John holds together the life given now and the resurrection still to come.
The figure of Daniel 7:13–14, who receives dominion from God. Jesus judges because he is the Son of Man: the judge of humanity is one who shared our humanity.
vv: anyone who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come under judgment, but has passed from death to life.
Faith in Christ is not only a ticket for the future; it is life already begun.
the hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.
Here “the dead” are those dead in sin. The Lord’s word raises them now; Lazarus (11:43) will be a visible sign of it.
Do not be astonished at this; for the hour is coming when all who are in their graves will hear his voice
Now the dead in the tombs. The verse echoes Daniel 12:2: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake.”
those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of condemnation.
This does not set works against faith. The good that leads to life is the fruit of grace received in faith (v. 24); our deeds matter because God’s grace truly works in us.
ch: St Augustine distinguishes two resurrections in this passage: the first now, when souls dead in sin hear the voice of the Son of God and rise by faith; the second at the end, when bodies come out of the tombs (in substance, City of God 20.6). The Catechism quotes vv. 28–29 when it teaches that the resurrection of all the dead, the just and the unjust, will precede the Last Judgment (CCC 1038).

qa: If believers “do not come under judgment”, why does v. 29 speak of judgment by deeds?

Both are true. The one who believes has already received life and is not condemned. But faith is living: it bears fruit in love, and a person can also turn away (Hebrews 3:12). At the end, Christ will reveal what each life has become. The Church teaches that our good works are themselves gifts of grace, and we hope for salvation by trusting in God’s mercy (CCC 1038–1041, 2008).
study: What is the Holy Spirit saying to me “today” that I keep postponing to tomorrow?
Whom could I encourage in faith this week, as Hebrews asks, “every day”?

lead: Both readings look beneath the surface. Paul reminds the Corinthians that he came to them not with polished rhetoric but with the message of Christ crucified, so that their faith would rest on God’s power and not on human cleverness. In Matthew, Jesus teaches that what defiles a person is not food taken in through the mouth but evil that comes out of the heart. God looks at the heart; the Cross is the power that changes it.

r.h: Nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified
set: Corinth was a rich, busy port city where public speakers were admired for their eloquence. Paul founded the Church there around AD 50–51, after his visit to Athens (Acts 17–18). By the time of this letter the Corinthians were dividing into parties around favourite preachers (1:12). Paul has just said that the message of the Cross is foolishness to the world but the power of God (1:18), and now he recalls how he first preached to them.
str: vv. 1–2: not lofty words; only Christ crucified.
v. 3: Paul’s own weakness and fear.
vv. 4–5: the Spirit and power, so that faith may rest on God.
kw: A real textual variant in v. 1. Some ancient manuscripts read “mystery”, others “testimony”. The NRSV follows “mystery”; the POC follows “testimony”. Both fit Paul’s thought.
A perfect participle: Christ remains the Crucified One. The risen Lord still bears his wounds (John 20:27).
A technical word of the schools of rhetoric for a convincing proof. Paul’s proof was not an argument but the work of the Spirit in the lives of those who believed.
vv: I did not come proclaiming the mystery of God to you in lofty words or wisdom.
Paul was not against learning; he was against anything that puts the preacher in place of the message.
For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
This is not a narrowing but a centre. Everything Paul teaches, the Resurrection included, flows from this.
And I came to you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling.
The great apostle was afraid. God’s strength showed itself in his weakness, as the Lord would tell him: “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
so that your faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God.
Faith built on a speaker’s charm falls when the speaker fails. Faith built on God stands.
ch: The Church has always read these verses as a rule for every preacher and catechist: the aim is not to win admiration but to bring people to Christ. St Augustine, himself a trained teacher of rhetoric, taught in On Christian Teaching that eloquence must serve truth and that the preacher’s life speaks louder than his words (in substance). The Catechism teaches that faith rests on the authority of God who reveals, not on the evidence of human reasoning alone (CCC 156).

r.h: What comes out of the heart
set: Some Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem have asked why Jesus’ disciples do not wash their hands before eating, as “the tradition of the elders” required (15:1–2). This ritual washing was a matter of religious purity, not hygiene. The Pharisees were devout men who wanted to bring holiness into daily life. Jesus’ dispute with them is a debate within Judaism about what God truly asks. Today’s reading is his answer, first to the crowd, then to the disciples.
str: vv. 10–11: to the crowd: not what goes in, but what comes out, defiles.
vv. 12–14: the disciples report the Pharisees’ offense; the plant not planted by the Father; blind guides.
vv. 15–20: to the disciples: the heart is the source of evil; washing hands does not defile.
kw: Literally “make common”, that is, unfit for what is holy. Jesus moves the question of holiness from the surface to the heart.
In the Bible, not only feelings but the inner centre of the person, where thought, will and decision are found.
Peter calls the saying a parable (v. 15): a short, puzzling word that needs to be opened. The disciples still need to be taught.
vv: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but it is what comes out of the mouth that defiles.
Words come from the heart. A person is known by what comes out of him: speech, attitudes, actions.
they are blind guides of the blind.
A warning to every teacher in the Church first of all. Those who guide others must first let themselves be enlightened.
But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this is what defiles.
Jesus does not despise outward practice; he teaches what gives it value.
to eat with unwashed hands does not defile.
Mark, telling the same story, adds that by this Jesus “declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). Matthew, probably writing for a community close to Jewish practice, keeps the focus on hand-washing.
ch: The list of evils in v. 19 largely follows the order of the second part of the Ten Commandments: murder, adultery, theft, false witness. Jesus is not abolishing the law but bringing it to the heart. The Catechism quotes this verse when it teaches that the heart is the seat of the moral personality (CCC 2517), and it says that the New Law purifies the heart, the root of human acts (CCC 1968).

study: Does my faith rest more on a favourite preacher or on the power of God? What would change if that preacher were gone?
Jesus says evil comes out of the heart. What have I said or done this week that shows me what my heart needs?
